In FaceVision, detection, embedding and liveness checks run entirely client-side via ONNX Runtime Web. The backend receives a 512-dimension embedding, never an image. If that backend is ever breached, there are no faces to steal — only vectors that can match, not reconstruct.
What you give up
Model size is constrained by what a browser can reasonably load and run, and you lose the ability to centrally update inference logic without a client update. For anything privacy-sensitive, that tradeoff is usually worth it.
Where this pattern applies beyond faces
Any input a user would reasonably not want stored — voice, handwriting, location patterns — is a candidate for on-device inference producing a derived, non-reversible representation instead of storing the raw input.

posts.title: Judging alongside non-technical co-judges: making a mixed panel actually work
posts.description: A panel with a technical judge and a business or design judge scores differently by default. How to align without flattening what each judge brings.
posts.text:
A panel mixing a technical judge with a business, design or domain-expert judge naturally scores execution differently — a technical judge spots a fragile demo instantly; a non-technical judge may not, and vice versa for market fit or usability.
Making a mixed panel work
Assign rubric criteria roughly to expertise during calibration — the technical judge weighs in more heavily on execution, the design judge on usability, both discuss impact together.
During calibration, have each judge explain what they're actually looking for in their area, so the others can spot it too.
Resist the urge to have the most confident voice dominate every criterion — the point of a mixed panel is the different lenses, not one lens amplified.
Why mixed panels are worth the coordination cost
A purely technical panel over-rewards clever engineering with no real user; a purely business panel under-rewards genuine technical difficulty. Together, properly calibrated, they score closer to what actually matters.
See panel judging vs solo judging.

posts.title: Liveness detection basics: stopping a photo from unlocking a face check
posts.description: Passive and active liveness, what attacks each stops, how to combine a small anti-spoofing model with motion challenges in the browser, and how to measure false accepts honestly.
posts.text:
A recognition model will happily match a printed photograph of you to your enrolled embedding. It was trained to recognise faces, not to notice paper. Liveness detection is the layer that asks "is there a live person here?" and FaceVision runs it in the browser alongside recognition.
Two families of liveness
Passive — a model looks at a single frame or a short clip for signs of a spoof: paper texture, screen moiré, unnatural depth cues. Frictionless for the user; only as good as its training data.
Active — the user is asked to do something: blink, turn their head, follow a dot. Cheap to implement with landmarks, hard to fool with a static photo, defeatable by a video replay unless the challenge is random.
Combine them
A passive check on every frame plus a randomised active challenge at enrolment and for high-value actions covers the common attacks: printed photos, phone screens, and pre-recorded videos. Neither alone does. Keep the challenge short — two actions — or users abandon the flow.
Doing it in the browser
Landmark tracking from the detector already gives you eye openness and head pose, so blink and turn challenges cost nothing extra. A small passive anti-spoofing model in ONNX runs in a worker alongside recognition. Frames stay on the device, which matters: liveness is where you would otherwise be streaming a user's face to a server continuously.
Measuring it honestly
Collect real spoof attempts — photos on paper, on a phone, a video on a laptop — from several people and devices.
Report the spoof acceptance rate and the live rejection rate separately. A system that rejects 20% of real users is not "secure", it is unusable.
Re-test whenever you change cameras, lighting assumptions or the model.
Liveness is the part of a face project that shows a reviewer you thought about how it would be attacked. Recognition gets the demo; liveness gets the job.

posts.title: When a team pushes back on your score: how to handle it without damaging trust
posts.description: Occasionally a team disagrees, sometimes loudly, with a judge's score. How to respond in a way that protects both the team's dignity and the process's integrity.
posts.text:
Occasionally a team disagrees, sometimes loudly, with a score — usually right after results are announced, when disappointment is freshest. How a judge responds in that moment matters for the team, the organiser, and the event's reputation.
How to handle it
Listen fully before responding — most of what a team needs in that moment is to be heard, not immediately corrected.
Point to the specific rubric criterion and what was and wasn't demonstrated, rather than a vague 'we felt it was weaker'.
If the team makes a fair point that genuinely wasn't considered, say so honestly — but don't change a published score after the fact just to placate frustration.
What not to do
Getting defensive or dismissive in the moment turns a disappointed team into one that feels wronged, which is worse for the event than the original disagreement. Calm, specific, rubric-anchored answers de-escalate almost every case.
See how judges should give feedback.

posts.title: Open source for students: contributing to AI repos without feeling lost
posts.description: How to make a first meaningful contribution to an AI or developer-tools repository: choosing a project you use, reading before writing, documentation and test contributions, and turning issues into a track record.
posts.text:
Open source is the most credible signal a student can produce, and the one most students never attempt because a large repository looks like a cliff. The way in is not heroics. It is contributing to something you already use, in the smallest way that is genuinely useful, and repeating.
Pick a repository you actually use
The retrieval library in your RAG project, the training toolkit in your fine-tuning project, the web framework in both. You already know its rough edges because you have hit them. That knowledge is your contribution.
Read before you write
The contributing guide and code of conduct.
Ten recent merged pull requests — what size, what style, what the maintainers ask for.
The issue tracker, filtered to labels like good first issue or documentation.
First contributions that are welcome
A documentation fix for something that confused you, with the clearer wording.
A reproducible bug report with a minimal example — often more valuable than a fix.
A test for behaviour that is not covered.
A small fix for an issue a maintainer has labelled as approachable.
How to behave
Comment on an issue before starting so nobody duplicates work. Keep the pull request small and single-purpose. Respond to review within a day and without defensiveness; review is teaching you the codebase. Thank people. Maintainers remember contributors who were easy to work with far more than those who were brilliant.
Turning it into a track record
Three merged contributions to a library you use is a line on your resume that no certificate matches, and a talking point in any interview: you have read production code and had your changes reviewed by its authors. Link the pull requests from your GitHub profile and mention them in your LinkedIn posts — the same visibility that leads to hackathon invitations and mentors.

posts.title: How to evaluate a fine-tuned model honestly (base vs tuned)
posts.description: If you can't show the before and after on the same prompts, you didn't fine-tune — you spent GPU hours. Here's how to evaluate properly.
posts.text:
The most common fine-tuning mistake I see isn't a bad hyperparameter — it's skipping evaluation entirely and assuming the loss curve going down means the model got better at the task you actually care about.
Run the same prompts through both models
Before touching the fine-tuned model, save a fixed set of representative prompts and the base model's answers to them. After training, run the identical prompts through the tuned model. Side by side, not from memory — memory of "how the base model used to answer" is unreliable after a training run.
Score what actually matters for your task
A general benchmark score tells you very little about whether the model got better at your specific narrow task. Write five to ten task-specific questions with known correct answers, and check both models against those.
What a real regression looks like
Sometimes the tuned model is worse on general knowledge and better on your task — that's expected and fine. Sometimes it's worse on both, which means something in the dataset or hyperparameters needs fixing before you ship it. You only find out which one happened if you actually run the comparison.

posts.title: Judge, mentor, or speaker — which one does your event actually need?
posts.description: The three roles look similar from the outside but need completely different preparation. Here's how to tell which one your event needs.
posts.text:
Organisers often ask for "a guest speaker" when what they actually need is a judge, or ask for a judge when a mentor would serve their students better. The three roles overlap, but they're not interchangeable.
A speaker informs a room
One-way, time-boxed, works for 50 to 500 people. Best when you want to introduce a topic — what RAG is, why fine-tuning matters, how the AI job market actually looks — to an audience that hasn't built anything yet.
A mentor invests in a smaller group over time
Best for a club or a final-year project team that needs ongoing feedback, not a single afternoon of inspiration. This is closest to what I've done at VSICS and through TechVerse Enclave — recurring contact, not a one-off visit.
A judge evaluates under pressure, once
Needs a transparent rubric shared with participants beforehand, not a gut-feel scorecard. If your event is a hackathon or a pitch competition, this is the role, and it's the one I'm most often asked for now given my own hackathon record on both sides of the table.
If you're not sure which you need
Tell me the format and the audience size, and I'll tell you honestly which role fits — sometimes it's a hybrid, a talk followed by judging the same event's pitches.

posts.title: Etiquette at the judges' table during live demos: what helps and what undermines a team
posts.description: Small things a judge does during a live demo — phone use, side conversations, facial reactions — visibly affect a nervous team's performance. What to actually do instead.
posts.text:
A nervous team pitching in front of a judges' table reads every small signal — a judge checking their phone, a side conversation, a confused frown — as feedback on the pitch itself, whether or not that's what the judge meant.
What helps a team perform their best
Full attention during the pitch itself — save note-writing for the gaps between sentences, not constant head-down scribbling.
A neutral, attentive expression rather than visible reactions mid-pitch, positive or negative — both can throw a nervous presenter off.
Asking questions that are genuinely about understanding the project, not testing whether the team can be rattled.
What undermines it
Side conversations between judges during a pitch are the single most common and most damaging habit — it visibly signals disinterest to a team that's already nervous, regardless of how the scoring actually goes.
See handling Q&A after a technical talk for the speaker's-side version of managing a room's attention.

posts.title: How face recognition works: embeddings, thresholds and why you never store faces
posts.description: Detection, alignment, embedding and matching explained without the maths, plus how to choose a similarity threshold, handle false matches, and design storage so a breach leaks numbers, not faces.
posts.text:
Face recognition is four steps, and only one of them is recognition. Understanding the pipeline is what lets you build one responsibly — which for FaceVision meant a system where the server has never seen a face.
The four steps
Detection — find faces in the frame and return bounding boxes and landmarks.
Alignment — rotate and crop each face to a canonical pose using the landmarks, so the next model sees consistent input.
Embedding — a recognition model maps the aligned face to a vector, typically 128 to 512 numbers, such that the same person's faces land close together.
Matching — compare the new embedding to stored ones with cosine similarity and decide with a threshold.
Choosing the threshold
Too strict and real users are rejected; too loose and strangers get in. Collect a small labelled set — pairs of the same person, pairs of different people — and plot the similarity distributions. The threshold sits where the curves separate; where they overlap is your error rate, and you should state it. Lighting, glasses and age change the distribution, so test with your actual users, not a benchmark.
Why you store embeddings, never images
An embedding is enough to verify a person and useless for showing anyone what they look like. Storing only embeddings — the FaceVision design — means a database breach leaks vectors rather than faces, consent conversations get simpler, and deletion is a single row. Run detection and embedding in the browser with ONNX Runtime Web and the raw image never leaves the device at all (see running ML models in the browser).
Failure modes to design for
A printed photo held up to the camera — this is why liveness detection exists.
Twins and look-alikes — accept that similarity is not identity and add a second factor for high-stakes actions.
Bias — recognition models perform unevenly across skin tones and ages; measure per group before deployment.
Build it this way and you can explain your system to a privacy officer in two sentences. That is a competitive advantage, not just an ethical one.

posts.title: Hackathon judging vs startup pitch judging: two different jobs that look similar
posts.description: Both involve a panel and a pitch, but a hackathon rewards a working 36-hour build; a startup pitch rewards a viable business. Judging one like the other misfires.
posts.text:
Both formats put a panel in front of a pitch and a demo, which makes it tempting to judge them the same way. The underlying question each format is actually asking is different.
What each is actually testing
Hackathon: did this team build something real, working, in a fixed short window — execution under time pressure is the core signal.
Startup pitch: is there a viable business here, with a market, a plan, and a team capable of executing it over years, not hours.
Where judges misfire
Applying startup-pitch criteria (market size, business model, go-to-market) to a 36-hour hackathon project punishes teams for not having solved a problem the format never asked them to solve. Judge each format on what it was actually designed to test.
See what hackathon judges look for for the hackathon-specific version of this criteria set.

posts.title: Learning Python for AI in 2026: the parts that matter
posts.description: The Python a GenAI engineer actually uses — data structures, async, typing, packaging, reading library code — and the parts students over-invest in, with a four-week plan built around a real project.
posts.text:
Students learning Python for AI spend months on syntax exercises and then cannot read the traceback from a library they installed. The Python that matters for building AI systems is narrower and deeper than the beginner courses suggest. Here is what I actually use, and a plan to learn it by building.
The parts that matter
Data structures fluently — dicts, lists, sets, comprehensions, and knowing when a generator saves your memory.
Functions and modules — writing code you can import, test and reuse; understanding what a package is.
Reading library code — opening the source of a retrieval or training library and following a call. This is the skill that separates users from engineers.
Async basics — enough to write a streaming endpoint and call several APIs concurrently.
Type hints — so your editor, your teammates and your future self can read the code.
Environments and dependencies — virtual environments, a lock file, and never installing globally.
Errors — reading a traceback bottom-up, writing exceptions that say what to do.
Over-invested
Advanced metaprogramming, decorators beyond the basics, and every dunder method.
Competitive-programming Python tricks that make code unreadable.
Memorising library APIs that change every release; learn to read their docs and source instead.
A four-week plan around one project
Week 1: a script that reads a PDF, splits it into chunks and writes JSON. Data structures and files.
Week 2: a FastAPI service that embeds and searches those chunks. Modules, typing, environments.
Week 3: a streaming answer endpoint calling an LLM API. Async, errors, logging.
Week 4: tests for the search, an evaluation script, a README. Packaging and reading library code when something breaks.
At the end you know the Python that a RAG system needs — because you built one — and you have the first project on the roadmap. The rest of the language you learn when a real problem asks for it.

posts.title: QLoRA fine-tuning: a complete guide for students
posts.description: What QLoRA actually does differently from full fine-tuning, why it fits on consumer hardware, and the steps to run your first job.
posts.text:
Full fine-tuning updates every parameter in a model, which for anything past a few billion parameters needs GPU memory most students don't have access to. QLoRA sidesteps this by quantizing the base model to 4-bit precision and training small, low-rank adapter matrices on top of it instead.
Why the memory savings are so large
The frozen base model in 4-bit takes a fraction of the memory of a full-precision copy, and the trainable adapters are tiny by comparison. That's how a 1.7B model fine-tunes at around 3.2 GB of peak VRAM instead of needing tens of gigabytes — the exact setup behind FineTune Studio.
The steps, in order
Validate your dataset first. Malformed examples fail loudly hours into training if you don't catch them at upload.
Pick a small base model appropriate to your task and hardware — bigger isn't automatically better for a narrow use case.
Set a learning rate and rank conservatively for a first run; QLoRA is forgiving, but not infinitely so.
Watch the loss curve live, not after the run finishes.
Evaluate base versus tuned on the same prompts. This step is the one people skip and shouldn't.
The honest tradeoff
QLoRA won't match full fine-tuning on every metric. For a narrow, well-defined task with a good dataset, the gap rarely matters — and it's the difference between a project you can actually run and one you can only read about.

posts.title: Judging a solo hacker's submission fairly against team submissions
posts.description: A solo participant is competing against teams of three or four with more hands and hours. Should the rubric adjust for that, and if so, how?
posts.text:
A solo participant produces less surface area — fewer features, a smaller demo — than a team of four with the same hours available, purely because there are fewer hands. Scoring them identically on raw scope isn't quite fair, but scoring generously just for being solo isn't fair to the teams either.
A workable approach
Keep the same rubric and weights for everyone — don't create a separate, softer bar for solo entrants.
Weight 'depth of execution on a smaller scope' as a legitimate strength within the existing execution criterion, rather than inventing a bonus category.
If solo participation is common at your event, consider a separate solo-hacker prize category instead of adjusting the main rubric.
What not to do
Silently mentally adjusting scores for solo participants without a stated rule creates exactly the inconsistency a rubric exists to prevent. If you're going to account for team size, make it an explicit, published rule.
See innovation vs execution: how I weigh a rubric.

posts.title: Running ML models in the browser with ONNX Runtime Web: a practical guide
posts.description: How to ship a vision model that runs entirely in the browser: exporting to ONNX, choosing WebGPU or WASM, pre- and post-processing pitfalls, and verifying the model against its reference implementation.
posts.text:
FaceVision does face detection, recognition and liveness checks without sending a single frame to a server, because every model runs in the browser through ONNX Runtime Web. That architecture is the reason its privacy story is simple. It is also the part students find hardest to get working, so here is the path that worked.
Export, then verify
Export the model to ONNX from its training framework and immediately run the same input through both the original and the exported graph. Compare outputs numerically. Every model in FaceVision was verified against its actual ONNX graph and, where possible, the reference implementation — not assumed from documentation. Half the "the model is broken in the browser" reports I have seen were pre-processing mismatches that a five-minute comparison would have caught.
Choose the execution provider deliberately
WebGPU — fastest where available; check support and fall back gracefully.
WASM with SIMD and threads — the reliable default; needs the right headers for multi-threading.
WebGL — legacy; avoid for new work.
Pre- and post-processing is where bugs live
Models expect a specific channel order, normalisation and input size. Browser image data arrives as RGBA bytes in a different layout. Write the conversion once, test it against a known image, and keep the output tensors' shapes in a comment next to the code. Post-processing — decoding anchors for a detector, normalising an embedding before cosine similarity — deserves the same care.
Performance that feels live
Warm up the session with one dummy inference on page load; the first run is always slow.
Run inference in a Web Worker so the camera preview never stutters.
Downscale frames before detection; run recognition only on detected crops.
Skip frames when the queue is full rather than letting latency grow.
What the backend does when the model does not
In FaceVision the FastAPI and PostgreSQL backend stores only vector embeddings and matches them at enrolment and verification. Because no images are ever persisted, the privacy claim is easy to explain and audit. I wrote about the design reasoning in face recognition that never uploads a face.
Browser-side inference is not a gimmick. For anything involving faces, documents or health data, it is often the architecture that makes the product acceptable to the people using it.

posts.title: Becoming a repeat hackathon judge: what organisers actually remember about you
posts.description: Organisers rarely remember a judge's exact scores. What they do remember — punctuality, written feedback quality, calm under a tight schedule — decides the next invite.
posts.text:
An organiser planning next year's hackathon rarely recalls a judge's exact scores from last year. What sticks is punctuality, the quality of written feedback, and whether the judge stayed calm and useful when the schedule slipped — which it always does.
What actually gets remembered
Showing up on time, prepared, having read the problem statements in advance.
Written feedback specific enough that a team quoted it back to the organiser afterward.
Flexibility when a session runs long or a team's slot moves — judges who complain about schedule slips are remembered for that, not their scoring.
The compounding effect
Being the easy, reliable judge to work with, repeated across several events, is what eventually gets a judge recommended by one organiser to another — which is how most judging invitations actually happen.
See how to become a hackathon judge.

posts.title: Internship, freelance or startup in Year 2?
posts.description: How a second-year student should choose between an internship, freelance client work and starting something — what each teaches, what each costs, and the combination that worked for the team behind SCULT INDIA.
posts.text:
Year 2 is when the roadmap I give first-years says "hackathons, internships, building in public", and it is when students ask me whether to intern, freelance or start a company. I did the last two while studying — SCULT INDIA began as three students shipping paid products — so my answer is not neutral, but it is honest about what each path teaches.
Internship
Teaches: how a real team works, code review, production systems you did not build, professional communication. Costs: your time is directed by someone else, and many student internships are low-value. Choose one where you will ship something with your name on it and can name a mentor. A good internship is the fastest way to learn what "production" means.
Freelance
Teaches: scoping, deadlines, invoicing, saying no, and what people will actually pay for. Costs: isolation, clients who change their minds, and the temptation to build the same website ten times. Choose projects that add a skill — a client who needs an AI feature, not a fifth landing page. SCULT INDIA's early paid products were exactly this.
Startup
Teaches: everything at once, badly at first. Costs: your grades if you are not careful, and your savings if you are not lucky. Start only if you already have a paying user or a real community — BrandHive won Product Genesis at CSJMU as a pitch; SCULT INDIA became a company because clients paid. The order matters.
The combination
Semester one of Year 2: one internship or two freelance projects, plus a hackathon.
Semester two: build in public on one project with real users; enter two hackathons as a team.
Summer: decide with evidence — did anyone pay, did anyone hire, what did you enjoy.
What not to do
Nothing. Year 2 with only coursework is the most expensive mistake on the roadmap, because Year 3 arrives with placement season and no evidence. Any of the three paths beats waiting; see what I told 100+ first-years for the full three-year plan.

posts.title: What a confidence gate is, and why every RAG app needs one
posts.description: A confidence gate stops an LLM from answering when retrieval comes back weak. Here's how to design the threshold and what it costs to skip it.
posts.text:
A confidence gate checks the top retrieved result's similarity score against a threshold before the language model is ever called. Fail the threshold, and the system returns a fixed refusal instead of letting the model improvise past its sources.
Why this has to happen before generation
Asking a model to self-assess its own confidence after answering means the system that might hallucinate is grading its own hallucination. A confidence gate checks the evidence, not the model's opinion of its own output — a check the model can't talk its way past.
Setting the threshold
Too high, and the system refuses paraphrased questions it could actually answer. Too low, and you're back to confident nonsense. There's no universal number — it has to be tuned against a real evaluation set of your own documents and your own users' phrasing.
The unexpected benefit: it's also a cost feature
Every refused call is a language-model call you didn't pay for. A well-tuned confidence gate reduces both hallucination and your API bill, which is a rare case of the safer choice also being the cheaper one.

posts.title: How I structure a free campus workshop (and why colleges should book one)
posts.description: What a hands-on session with me actually looks like on the ground: live system, real repo, one takeaway students can act on that week.
posts.text:
Placement cells and student clubs often assume a "guest speaker" means an hour of slides. That's not what I run, and it's worth spelling out exactly what a session with me looks like before you invite one.
No slide-only talks
Every session has a live system on screen — the RAG platform answering a real question with citations, the fine-tuning dashboard streaming loss in real time — and a repo students can clone the same evening. Abstract claims about AI are cheap; a working demo is not.
Real numbers, not adjectives
Memory limits, VRAM figures, test counts, what the API bill actually looks like. Students remember "220 MB on a free tier" far longer than they remember "lightweight and efficient."
One takeaway, always
Every session ends with something students can act on that week: ship the ugliest working version of one idea, deploy it publicly, write 500 honest words about what broke. That loop, repeated, is the entire method behind everything I've built.
What it costs your college
Nothing, for student communities and public colleges. A projector, wifi, and laptops if it's a hands-on workshop. See the full talk menu and how to invite me at the link below.

posts.title: Ten fine-tuning mistakes I see students make (and made myself)
posts.description: The mistakes that turn a fine-tuning project into a shrug: no baseline, dirty data, the wrong metric, training on eval data, chasing loss, and skipping the deployment question.
posts.text:
I built FineTune Studio after making most of these mistakes on my own runs. They are not exotic. They are the difference between "I fine-tuned a model" on a resume and "I fine-tuned a model and here is what improved by how much".
The mistakes
No baseline. Not running the base model on the same evaluation set first. Without it, you cannot know whether the fine-tune did anything. Base-versus-tuned is the whole point.
Training on unvalidated data. Malformed records, duplicates, and template mismatches. Run the pre-training checklist first.
Leaking eval into training. Splitting after deduplication is not optional.
Chasing training loss. It goes down whether or not the model is getting better. Watch eval loss, then read outputs.
Too many epochs on too little data. A few hundred examples for ten epochs is memorisation with a progress bar.
Choosing the biggest model that fits. A 1–3B model fine-tuned well beats a 7B model fine-tuned badly, and ships on hardware you have.
Fine-tuning for facts. Knowledge belongs in retrieval; see RAG vs fine-tuning.
Ignoring the chat template. Training with one format and serving with another produces a model that seems to have forgotten everything.
Not saving checkpoints. The best model was at step 600; you only kept step 1200.
No deployment plan. An adapter on a laptop is not a result anyone else can use. Decide how it will be served before you start.
The habit that prevents most of them
Write the evaluation before the training script: the held-out set, the rubric, and the baseline numbers. Everything else becomes an experiment against a fixed target instead of a hope. That habit, more than any hyperparameter, is what I try to teach in campus sessions on fine-tuning.
Make these mistakes once, on a small model, on a weekend. Then never again.

posts.title: What a hackathon judge should include in a post-event report to organisers
posts.description: Beyond the scores, a short report back to organisers on rubric gaps, standout teams and process friction helps the next event run better than this one.
posts.text:
Most judges submit scores and leave. A short post-event report back to organisers — separate from the per-team feedback — is one of the most useful and least common things a judge can offer.
What to include
Where the rubric felt ambiguous or produced inconsistent scores across the panel, so it can be tightened next time.
Any logistics friction — scheduling, room setup, briefing gaps — from the judge's side of the table.
One or two standout teams worth following up with beyond the prize, if any showed unusual promise.
Why organisers value this
Organisers rarely get structured feedback on their own process, only on the event's atmosphere. A judge who reports back on the mechanics is doing genuinely rare, valuable work — and it's part of why that judge gets invited back.
See what a judges' briefing should cover for the input side of this same feedback loop.

posts.title: Judging a virtual hackathon with teams across time zones
posts.description: A global online hackathon spreads teams across a dozen time zones. What that actually changes about scheduling, fatigue and fairness for judges.
posts.text:
A virtual hackathon open to teams worldwide spreads submissions and live pitches across a dozen time zones, and pretending a single judging slot works for everyone produces an exhausted panel and a jet-lagged one-size-fits-none schedule.
What actually needs planning
Stagger pitch slots across a wider window (12+ hours) with judges rotating shifts, rather than one panel sitting through all of it.
Accept asynchronous submissions (a recorded demo) as an equally valid format alongside live pitches, since 'live' disadvantages teams in inconvenient time zones.
Score against the same rubric regardless of format — a recorded demo shouldn't be penalised structurally for not being live.
Protecting judge quality across long or odd-hour shifts
Cap each judge's shift at the same 12-15 pitch limit that applies to in-person judging (see how many teams can one judge fairly see) — a virtual format doesn't remove the attention limit, it just makes it easier to ignore.

posts.title: LinkedIn for CS students: posting projects without cringe
posts.description: How to use LinkedIn as a student engineer: what to post, how often, the post structure that gets replies from practitioners, and what to avoid — from someone whose posts led to talks, judging invitations and clients.
posts.text:
Every session I have given, every judging invitation and several SCULT INDIA clients trace back to something I posted on LinkedIn about a project or a hackathon. Students know this and still hesitate, because most student posts they see are either bragging or begging. There is a third mode, and it is the one that works.
Post what you built and what broke
The structure: what problem, what you built, one thing that went wrong, one number, one question for the reader. "We won" is fine once; "here is what the judges asked and what we cut" is the post practitioners reply to. My STROT posts about a hackathon we did not win reached more people than the winning ones.
A cadence you can keep
One project post a fortnight while you are building.
One event post per hackathon, session or talk — with photographs of the room, not only the certificate.
One lesson post a month: something you got wrong and understand now.
What gets replies from people who matter
A working link in the post.
A specific question at the end that a practitioner can answer in one line.
Tagging the institute or community by name, correctly.
Replying to every comment within a day.
What to avoid
"Humbled and honoured" openers.
Certificates as the only content.
Motivational text with no project behind it.
Asking for a job in the comments of a stranger's post.
Why it matters beyond jobs
Posting is how colleges find guest speakers, how organisers find judges, and how communities find mentors. My campus invite page exists because posts created the demand for it. Start in Year 1 with a small project; by Year 3 you have a record nobody can fake. The wider plan is in building your personal brand as a CS student.

posts.title: Hybrid retrieval explained: dense search, BM25, and Reciprocal Rank Fusion
posts.description: Why combining vector search with keyword search beats either alone, and how Reciprocal Rank Fusion merges the two without score normalisation headaches.
posts.text:
Dense vector search is good at meaning. Ask about "a smart farming assistant" and it'll find a chunk about "an AI agribot for real-time guidance" even without a shared word. But it's bad at exact strings — a specific product SKU, an error code, a number — because those don't carry semantic meaning the way concepts do.
BM25 covers the gap
BM25 is decades-old keyword search, and it's still the right tool for exact-term matching. Run it alongside dense search, not instead of it.
Merging two ranked lists without breaking anything
The naive approach — averaging similarity scores from two different systems — breaks because the score scales aren't comparable. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) sidesteps this entirely: each chunk's fused score is the sum of `1 / (k + rank)` across every list it appears in. No normalisation needed, because rank position, not score magnitude, is what's being combined.
When hybrid retrieval actually matters
If your documents contain product names, version numbers, or specific figures a user might search verbatim, hybrid retrieval isn't optional — pure vector search will silently miss exact queries and you may never notice, because the wrong answer still sounds plausible.

posts.title: Instruction tuning vs domain adaptation: two different fine-tuning goals
posts.description: Teaching a model to follow your instructions is not the same as teaching it your domain's language. How the data, the training objective and the evaluation differ, and how to avoid mixing them badly.
posts.text:
"Fine-tune it on our data" hides two different requests. One is: make the model behave the way we want when asked. The other is: make the model fluent in our field. They need different datasets, different training setups and different tests. Confusing them is the most common design error I see in student projects.
Instruction tuning
The data is pairs — or conversations — of request and ideal response. The loss is computed on the response tokens. The goal is behaviour: follow the format, respect the constraints, respond in the house tone. A few thousand carefully written examples go a long way. This is what most QLoRA projects in FineTune Studio are.
Domain adaptation
The data is raw text from the field — manuals, papers, transcripts — and the loss is computed on all of it, the way the base model was pre-trained. The goal is vocabulary and fluency: the model stops stumbling over your acronyms. It needs far more text, and it does not by itself teach the model to answer questions politely. Usually you follow it with a short instruction-tuning stage.
How they differ in practice
Data volume — thousands of examples versus millions of tokens.
Loss masking — response-only versus full sequence.
Evaluation — task rubric on held-out instructions versus perplexity on held-out domain text, then task rubric after the instruction stage.
Risk — instruction tuning can overfit to phrasing; domain adaptation can erode general instruction-following if pushed too far.
What you probably want
If your problem is facts, neither — use retrieval, as argued in RAG vs fine-tuning. If your problem is behaviour, instruction tuning. If the model genuinely cannot read your domain's text, a modest domain-adaptation pass followed by instruction tuning. Decide which before you collect data, because the data you need is different.
Name the goal, and the recipe follows. Skip that step and you will train the wrong thing perfectly.

posts.title: Building credibility as a speaker before you've ever given a college talk
posts.description: Nobody gets a first invite from nowhere. What to build first — publicly — so a fest team has a reason to trust an unproven speaker with their audience.
posts.text:
Nobody gets invited to speak from nowhere. A fest team booking an unproven speaker needs some public evidence of judgement and communication ability before taking that risk.
What builds that evidence, before a single invite
Writing publicly about what you're building or have learned — it's the cheapest, most durable evidence of clear thinking available to anyone.
Speaking at a smaller, lower-stakes venue first: your own club, a meetup, a smaller local event.
Being visibly active and helpful in a community — answering questions well, mentoring informally — before ever asking for a stage.
The first invite usually comes from someone who already saw this evidence
It rarely comes cold from a stranger scanning profiles — it comes from someone who already read a post, saw an answer you gave, or watched you help someone else. Build that trail first.
See why I write and publish.

posts.title: A GitHub profile recruiters actually read
posts.description: How to arrange a GitHub profile so a reviewer finds the right three projects in thirty seconds: pins, a profile README with numbers, project READMEs that lead with the problem, and what to archive.
posts.text:
Recruiters and mentors spend about thirty seconds on a GitHub profile before deciding whether to spend five minutes. Most student profiles waste those seconds on a wall of tutorial repositories. Mine has 24 public repositories; three of them do the work, and the profile is arranged so those three are what you see.
Pin three, not six
One retrieval project, one fine-tuning or vision project, one with real users. Pinned repositories are the whole first impression; six dilute it. Each pinned repository needs a description line that states the problem, not the stack.
The profile README
One line of positioning and where you are based.
Three projects with a one-line outcome each and a link — the same three that are pinned.
Wins and sessions with institutes and years.
How to reach you. An email, not a contact form.
Project READMEs that survive ninety seconds
First line: the problem and who has it.
A screenshot or a short recording of it running.
The numbers: users, evaluation results, performance.
How it works, in one diagram or five bullets.
How to run it, and a link to where it is running.
What you would do next, honestly.
Archive the rest
Tutorial clones, abandoned experiments and forks you never touched can be archived or made private. A profile with five good repositories reads as focused; one with forty half-finished ones reads as noise, however hard you worked on each.
Commit history is read too
Regular, descriptive commits over months signal someone who ships. A single "final version" commit signals a copy. Push as you build — it is also the habit that saves you when a laptop dies the night before a demo.
Fix the profile in an evening, then keep it current with each project from the roadmap. It is the first thing I open when a student asks me for feedback, and the first thing a recruiter opens when they consider an interview.

posts.title: RAG systems: a complete beginner's guide (2026)
posts.description: What retrieval-augmented generation actually is, why it exists, and the components a real RAG system needs beyond a vector database.
posts.text:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) exists to solve one problem: language models don't know your data, and retraining one every time your documents change isn't realistic. RAG instead retrieves relevant text at query time and hands it to the model as context.
The minimum viable pipeline
Ingest your documents — split them into chunks small enough to retrieve precisely, large enough to keep context.
Embed each chunk into a vector and store it in a vector database.
Retrieve the chunks most similar to a user's query.
Generate an answer, with the retrieved chunks in the prompt.
Where beginners stop, and where production starts
That four-step pipeline works in a demo and falls apart on real questions. Production RAG needs hybrid retrieval (vector search alone misses exact terms like product names), reranking (a second, more precise pass over the top candidates), and a confidence threshold that refuses to answer when nothing retrieved is actually relevant. I cover the last one in detail in why my RAG platform says "I don't know".
The one mistake that wastes the most time
Building the pipeline before building an evaluation set. Without a fixed set of question-answer pairs with known correct sources, every change you make is a guess dressed up as an improvement.

posts.title: Sharing a stage: co-speaking with another guest at the same college event
posts.description: A fest sometimes books two speakers for the same slot or back to back. Coordinating with the other speaker beforehand turns overlap into a stronger combined session.
posts.text:
A fest occasionally books two speakers for the same session or back-to-back slots without checking whether their content overlaps. Left uncoordinated, the audience hears the same idea twice; coordinated beforehand, the two talks reinforce each other.
What to actually coordinate
A quick message before the event: what's each of you covering, so there's no accidental duplication.
Who goes first, and whether the second speaker should reference the first's points.
Whether a joint Q&A at the end makes sense, or two separate slots serve the audience better.
The upside of doing this well
Two well-coordinated speakers back to back give an audience genuine breadth — one might cover the build, the other the career path — which is a stronger session than either speaker could deliver alone.
See how I prepare a campus talk for the individual-prep half this builds on.

posts.title: From adapter to deployment: merging LoRA weights and serving with vLLM or a Space
posts.description: What to do after training: keep or merge the adapter, choose between local inference, a vLLM server and a hosted Space, and check that the served model matches what you evaluated.
posts.text:
A fine-tuned adapter sitting in a folder is not a product. FineTune Studio offers three inference paths — local, a vLLM server, or a Hugging Face Space — because the right one depends on who will call the model and how often. Here is how I choose, and the checks I run before calling it deployed.
Keep the adapter or merge it?
Keeping the adapter separate lets you hot-swap behaviours on one base model and keeps files small. Merging bakes the adapter into the base weights, producing a single model that any serving stack can load without adapter support. Merge when you have one behaviour and want simplicity; keep adapters when you serve several tasks from one base.
Three serving paths
Local inference — the training machine loads the model and answers requests. Right for demos, evaluation and internal tools; wrong for anything with real traffic.
vLLM server — batched, fast, OpenAI-compatible API. Right for production on a GPU you control. Supports LoRA adapters directly, so merging is optional.
Hosted Space — a public or gated endpoint for sharing a demo. Right for portfolios and hackathon judges; be mindful of cold starts and free-tier limits.
Checks before you call it shipped
The served model reproduces your evaluation outputs. Precision differences and a missing chat template produce a subtly different model.
The chat template used at serving time is the one used in training.
Stop tokens are configured; otherwise the model talks until the token limit.
Throughput and memory are measured with realistic concurrency, not one request at a time.
Operating it
Put the endpoint behind the same reliability layer as any LLM API: timeouts, retries, structured logs with the model version in every record. A fine-tuned model is a dependency you now maintain; version the adapter, the dataset and the evaluation results together so you can answer "what changed?" six months later.
Training is the exciting half. Serving is the half that makes it real, and it is where students separate themselves from tutorial followers.

posts.title: When a college cancels your session at the last minute: how to handle it well
posts.description: Fest schedules slip and sessions get cancelled or moved with little notice. A gracious response protects the relationship for next time, far more than the cancellation itself matters.
posts.text:
Fest schedules slip constantly — a keynote runs long, a venue falls through, and your session gets cancelled or moved with almost no notice. How you respond matters more for the relationship than the cancellation itself.
The response that protects the relationship
Respond with understanding, not frustration — organisers are usually more stressed about the cancellation than you are.
Offer a genuine alternative: a remote follow-up session, a shorter slot the next day, a recorded version instead.
Don't invoice or push back on a free session's cancellation — the goodwill from being easy to work with here outweighs any lost prep time.
What this earns you
Organisers remember who was gracious about a bad situation, and gracious speakers are the ones they call again despite the earlier mess.
See what makes a college invite the same speaker back.

posts.title: Why I judge a hackathon pitch on storytelling as much as code
posts.description: Three hackathon wins and a loss on a two-minute pitch taught me the same thing from opposite sides of the judging table.
posts.text:
I've been on both sides of a hackathon scoreboard — three first prizes, a top-3 finish, and one loss I still think about (STROT, judged on a two-minute pitch for a system that took two days to build). That combination is exactly why I judge pitches the way I do when I'm invited to sit on the other side of the table.
What I actually score
Can I explain this system back to you in one sentence after your pitch? If not, the idea isn't the problem — the communication is.
Does the demo work live? A slide of a screenshot is not a demo.
Did the team make a real tradeoff on purpose? "We didn't have time for X so we did Y instead, because Z" tells me more than a feature list.
What I don't over-weight
Framework choice. I've seen React Flask judged harshly next to a flashier stack solving a weaker problem. The technology is a means, and judges who forget that end up rewarding the wrong thing.
If you want me on your panel
I judge student hackathons on-site or remote, and I bring this exact rubric — transparent, and shared with organisers ahead of time so nobody's scored on a hidden standard.

posts.title: A resume for AI roles as a fresher: what to put above the fold
posts.description: How to structure a one-page resume for GenAI and AI engineering roles when you have no full-time experience: projects with numbers first, a skills line that matches job posts, and what to cut.
posts.text:
A fresher's resume for an AI role has one job: make the reviewer open a project link in the first fifteen seconds. Most resumes I see in placement clinics bury the projects under a college header and a paragraph of adjectives. Here is the order that works, from what I have seen get callbacks.
Above the fold
Name, one-line positioning, links. "GenAI engineer · RAG, fine-tuning, production AI apps" and clickable GitHub, LinkedIn and portfolio links. No address, no photo.
Three projects, each in three lines: what problem, what you built (with the stack), one number — users, evaluation score, latency, VRAM. A link on each title.
Skills, one dense line grouped by area, matching the vocabulary of the job posts you are applying to.
Below the fold
Wins and talks — hackathon prizes with the institute and year, sessions you delivered. These are evidence of initiative; they belong on the page.
Education, one line. Degree, institution, year. Grades only if strong.
Community and open source, if real.
Writing the project lines
Bad: "Developed an AI-powered chatbot using the latest technologies." Good: "Built a RAG assistant over 400 pages of department notes; hybrid retrieval + reranking + confidence gate; recall@5 0.91 on a 60-question set; 40 weekly users." The second is longer and takes less time to evaluate.
Cut
The objective paragraph.
Soft-skill lists.
Courses and certificates unless the role requires one.
Anything you cannot talk about for five minutes.
Match, then send
Read three job posts for the role, note the words they repeat — retrieval, evaluation, LLM APIs, FastAPI — and make sure the resume uses them where true. Then send it with the portfolio it points to, because the resume is only the doorway; the projects in five AI portfolio projects that get interviews are the room.

posts.title: Turning a single guest lecture into an ongoing mentor relationship with a student
posts.description: Most guest lectures end when the session does. A few students always ask a follow-up question — what happens after that first message decides everything.
posts.text:
Most guest lectures end the moment the session does. A few students always send a follow-up message afterward — what happens in that first reply decides whether it becomes an ongoing mentor relationship or a dead end.
What that first reply should do
Answer the actual question asked, specifically, rather than a generic 'keep learning' response.
End with one small, concrete next step for the student to try.
Leave the door open explicitly — 'let me know how it goes' invites the next message far better than silence does.
Where it goes from there
A student who reports back on that next step is showing exactly the habit that makes a mentor keep investing — see what a good mentee does. The relationship compounds one honest exchange at a time, not from a single big gesture.

posts.title: Small language models (1B–3B): what they're good for after fine-tuning
posts.description: Where small open models genuinely beat frontier APIs after a fine-tune — classification, extraction, routing, on-device tasks — and where they still fall short, from someone who ships them.
posts.text:
A 1.7B-parameter model will not write your thesis. It will, after fine-tuning, classify ten thousand support tickets an hour on a CPU, for free, without sending customer data anywhere. FineTune Studio is built around small models because that trade is the one most teams actually need.
Where small models win
Classification and routing — intent detection, ticket triage, deciding which expensive model a request deserves. Fine-tuned small models are consistent and cheap here.
Structured extraction — pulling fields from a known document type into a schema. Pair with validation and you have a deterministic pipeline.
Format enforcement — producing strict JSON, a house style, or a fixed template every time.
Privacy-bound tasks — anything that must not leave the server or the device.
Latency-bound tasks — sub-second responses on modest hardware.
Where they still lose
Open-ended reasoning across long contexts.
Knowledge-heavy questions — use retrieval, not parameters, for facts (see RAG vs fine-tuning).
Tasks with few examples; small models need the data to learn the behaviour.
A pattern that works in production
A fine-tuned small model in front, doing the cheap, frequent, narrow work; a frontier API behind it for the hard cases it flags. Costs drop, latency drops, and the expensive model is used where it matters. Multi-provider fallback, as in RAG.NextUpgrad, keeps the expensive path reliable.
How to prove it
Train on your data, then run the base model, the tuned model and the frontier API on the same held-out set and score them with the same rubric. When the tuned 1.7B model matches the API on your task at a fraction of the cost, you have a result worth putting in a portfolio — and a talking point for any GenAI interview.

posts.title: Mentoring through a college's alumni network instead of one-off visits
posts.description: Some colleges have a standing alumni-mentor structure. Plugging into it, rather than only doing one-off guest talks, changes the kind of impact you can have.
posts.text:
Some colleges run a standing alumni-mentor structure — a pool of past students or friendly practitioners available for ongoing questions, not just a one-off guest slot. Plugging into this changes what kind of impact is possible.
What's different about this structure
Students reach out on their own schedule, not just during a scheduled visit — mentoring becomes continuous rather than event-shaped.
The relationship can span years, following one student from first year through placements or a startup decision.
It requires less prep per interaction but more ongoing availability than a single talk.
Offering to join one, even without a formal invite
Most colleges without a formal alumni-mentor programme are happy to start an informal version if a practitioner offers — a shared channel, a monthly office hour, open to any student who wants in.
See office hours for students: how I run them.

posts.title: From a non-IIT college to AI engineer: a realistic path
posts.description: What an engineering student in a tier-2 city can do to reach a GenAI engineering role: the syllabus gaps and how to fill them, where the opportunities are, and Pranjul Rathour's own path from VSICS.
posts.text:
I studied computer applications at Dr. Virendra Swarup Institute of Computer Studies, not at an IIT. By the end of it I was the GenAI engineer for an AI-first studio, had won three hackathons — two of them at IIT Roorkee and CSJMU — and had shipped five production AI apps. None of that was on the syllabus. Here is the path as I would describe it to an engineering student today, without the motivational gloss.
Know the gaps
A typical tier-2 college syllabus gives you programming fundamentals, databases and a project. It usually does not give you Python at production depth, deployment, version control as a habit, or anything current in AI. Those are the gaps; they are all fillable outside class, and most of them in a semester.
Fill them with projects, in order
A deployed web app with a database — the floor.
A RAG project with evaluation numbers over something local: your college's documents, a shop's catalogue.
One fine-tuning or vision project on free hardware.
One of them taken to real users.
That is the GenAI engineer roadmap, and it does not care which college you attend.
Where the opportunities actually are
Hackathons at bigger institutes are open to everyone. Krishi Gyan won Changethon at IIT Roorkee as a team from a tier-2 college.
Local communities — MeetKats ran BYTEBATTLE, which Annapurna won. Every city has one.
Remote roles and startups judge the repository, not the campus; see getting a remote GenAI role from a tier-2 city.
Freelance and client work — SCULT INDIA started as three students shipping paid products.
What the college does give you
Time, a peer group and a stage. TechVerse Enclave started as a few students at VSICS helping each other build; the college gave us a seminar hall for the AI Mentorship Session and the induction. Use the institution for what it is good at — community and rooms — and the internet for the rest.
The honest part
Campus placements at a non-IIT college will offer fewer AI roles. That is a reason to build a visible portfolio early, not a reason to give up on the field. The recruiters who found me found projects and posts, not a college name.

posts.title: Why I speak at colleges for free
posts.description: The economics of free campus talks, and why I still say yes to almost every student community that asks.
posts.text:
Every session I run for a student community or a public college is free. That's a deliberate choice, not a placeholder until I start charging.
The actual return
TechVerse Enclave exists because a handful of people said yes to unglamorous, unpaid sessions early on. The 200+ students I've mentored didn't arrive because of a marketing budget — they arrived because someone showed up for their college first. That compounds in ways a speaking fee never would.
Where the line is
Free for students and public institutions. Corporate workshops and paid consulting are a different conversation — write in and we'll figure out what's fair for both sides.
What I ask in return
Nothing beyond an audience that's actually willing to build something during the session. I'll bring the content and the live demo. You bring the room.

posts.title: How I keep track of every college I've spoken at (and why it matters more than it sounds)
posts.description: A simple spreadsheet of college, date, topic and outcome prevents repeated talks, missed follow-ups, and forgotten relationships as the number of sessions grows.
posts.text:
After a handful of sessions, remembering which college heard which talk, and whether a follow-up happened, becomes genuinely hard without a system. A simple log fixes this permanently.
What goes in the log
College, date, format (talk, workshop, mentorship session), topic covered.
Coordinator name and contact — this is what makes a repeat invite a warm reintroduction instead of a cold one.
Any promised follow-up and whether it happened.
A rough outcome note, if you heard one — projects shipped, a club that grew, nothing heard back.
Why this matters more than it sounds
It's the difference between 'have I spoken here before?' being a guess and being an instant, confident answer — which matters the moment a coordinator writes 'we'd love to have you back'.
See measuring the impact of a campus session for the outcome-tracking half of this same habit.

posts.title: Validate your dataset before you burn a GPU hour: a checklist
posts.description: A pre-training checklist for fine-tuning datasets: schema, roles, duplicates, leakage, length distribution, label balance and the rendered-template spot check that catches what scripts miss.
posts.text:
Most fine-tuning failures I have seen were dataset failures: malformed records, duplicated examples, a prompt template mismatch. FineTune Studio validates on upload precisely because a clear error before training is worth more than any dashboard during it. Here is the checklist it implements, so you can run it yourself.
Structure
Every record parses, and every record has the same shape. One stray field name breaks tokenisation silently.
Roles alternate correctly and every conversation ends with an assistant turn — that is the turn you train on.
No empty assistant messages. They teach the model that silence is an answer.
Content
Exact and near-duplicate examples removed. Duplicates make the loss look great and the model brittle.
No overlap between training and evaluation splits — check by hashing normalised text, not by hoping.
Length distribution inspected: a handful of 8,000-token examples will set your sequence length and your memory bill. Truncate or drop them deliberately.
Label or intent balance checked for classification-style data; a 95/5 split trains a model that always says the 95.
Rendering
Render twenty random examples through the exact chat template you will train with, decode them back to text, and read them. This catches the mistakes scripts cannot: system prompts duplicated on every turn, a stray instruction inside an answer, examples in the wrong language. Formats and templates are covered in fine-tuning datasets without the confusion.
Provenance
Know where every example came from and whether you are allowed to train on it. Client data needs consent; scraped data needs a licence check. Write the source into the dataset card. A model you cannot explain the training data for is a model you cannot ship to a client.
Then, and only then
Start the run and watch the loss curve. A validated dataset turns a mysterious training failure into a hyperparameter question, and hyperparameter questions have answers.

posts.title: The speaker kit: photos, video clips and copy organisers actually ask for
posts.description: A promo poster needs a decent photo and a short bio within the hour it's requested. Having a ready speaker kit turns a same-day ask into a five-minute reply.
posts.text:
An organiser building a promo poster the night before a fest needs a decent photo and a short bio right now, not next week. Having these ready in advance turns a stressful same-day ask into a five-minute reply.
What to keep ready
A high-resolution, face-clear photo, landscape and portrait crops both, so it fits any poster layout.
A 30-word and a 60-word bio, so an organiser can pick whichever fits their design.
A short clip from a past session, if you have one — organisers use these for social promotion far more than a static photo.
Where to keep it
One folder, one link, sent proactively when you confirm a session rather than waiting to be asked. It's a small thing that makes organisers' lives noticeably easier.
See the speaker one-pager for where this kit fits alongside the logistics page.

posts.title: Five AI portfolio projects that get interviews (and five that don't)
posts.description: From reviewing hundreds of student portfolios: the projects that make a reviewer lean forward, the ones that get skipped, and the three things that turn any project into an interview.
posts.text:
I have reviewed hundreds of student portfolios through TechVerse Enclave, placement clinics and hiring at SCULT INDIA. Most contain the same three projects, and reviewers skip them in seconds. The ones that get interviews are not harder; they are more honest about a real problem.
Projects that get interviews
A RAG system with published evaluation numbers over a corpus you understand — recall, faithfulness, refusal rate. The numbers are the differentiator.
A fine-tuned small model with a base-versus-tuned comparison on a task you can explain in one sentence.
A document or vision tool with a validation layer — extraction plus arithmetic checks, or recognition plus liveness. Shows you think about failure.
Anything with ten real users and a changelog driven by their feedback. A shop, a club, an NGO.
A tool you built for yourself and still use. Reviewers can tell.
Projects that get skipped
The chatbot with no retrieval and no evaluation.
The tutorial clone with the tutorial's dataset.
The dashboard with fake data and no user.
The "AI-powered" app where the AI is one prompt and the rest is a template.
Anything without a README that says what problem it solves in the first line.
Three things that turn any project into an interview
A URL. Something running, even on a free tier, beats a perfect repository nobody can try.
Numbers. Users, evaluation scores, latency, cost. Any honest number.
A trade-off, stated. "We chose X over Y because Z" is the sentence reviewers remember.
How many projects
Three good ones beat twelve. One retrieval, one fine-tuning or vision, one with real users — the shape of the roadmap. Then spend the remaining time on the READMEs, because a reviewer gives each project about ninety seconds, and the README is where that time goes.

posts.title: Losing a hackathon well: what to keep, what to ditch
posts.description: How to lose a hackathon and come out ahead: reading the judges' feedback, separating the pitch problem from the product problem, and why STROT taught more than three first prizes.
posts.text:
We did not win with STROT. Two nights, almost no sleep, a system we believed in, and a two-minute pitch that did not land. I have written about the pitch lesson before; this is about the hour after the results, because that hour decides what the loss is worth.
First, do nothing for a day
Sleep-deprived analysis is unreliable. Thank the organisers, congratulate the winners sincerely, and go home. The team that argues with judges at the venue is remembered for that, not for the project.
Then separate two questions
Was it a pitch problem? The judges did not understand what you built or why it mattered. Fixable in two weeks of rehearsal; the product may be fine.
Was it a product problem? The judges understood it and did not think it solved a real problem, or the demo did not work. Harder, and more important to face.
For STROT it was mostly the first. The system was real; the story was too abstract for two minutes. That diagnosis changed how I coach every team I mentor now.
Read the feedback twice
Once to react, once to extract. Write each comment as a neutral observation, then decide whether it is true. The criticisms that sting most are usually the ones with something in them. Ask a judge afterwards if you can — most will give five honest minutes to a team that asks well.
Keep, ditch, decide
Keep the problem if users still have it. Losing does not make the problem go away.
Ditch the parts you built to impress judges rather than to serve users.
Decide within two weeks whether to keep shipping or to archive properly — see after the hackathon.
What a loss gives you
A story with a lesson in it, which is worth more in an interview or a talk than a trophy with no story. When I speak at colleges, students remember the STROT slide more than the three wins. Losing well is a skill, and it is one worth practising early.

posts.title: STROT: the hackathon I didn't win, and the pitch lesson that mattered more
posts.description: We lost this one with a two-minute pitch for a system that took days to build. Clarity beat depth, and that lesson has outlasted every trophy.
posts.text:
In December 2025 my team built STROT, a system-driven platform aimed at tackling generational poverty through what we called "BAL. BUDDHI. VIDYA." We didn't win the hackathon. We walked out with something more useful: a specific, painful lesson about pitching.
The problem wasn't the system
We had a product, a story and a vision. What we didn't have was a way to explain a system that takes hours to understand in the two minutes the stage gave us. Judges scored the pitch they heard, not the system we'd actually built — and they were right to.
Three lessons I still use
Clarity matters more than depth. A judge who doesn't understand the core loop in thirty seconds won't score the rest of the pitch fairly, no matter how good it is.
Storytelling matters as much as systems. The most technically impressive project I've built is not automatically the one that communicates best under a countdown timer.
Every stage builds you for the next one. The pitch skills from Product Genesis and BYTEBATTLE didn't transfer perfectly to a two-minute format, and that gap was worth learning before it cost me something bigger.
We didn't take the trophy, but we took the product forward — because an idea like STROT deserves more than a scoreboard.

posts.title: Building an ongoing relationship with several college tech clubs at once
posts.description: One-off talks are fine. A standing relationship with a handful of clubs — where they come back every semester — compounds far more for both sides.
posts.text:
A one-off talk is a fine start. A standing relationship with a handful of clubs — where the same coordinator emails you every semester — is where mentoring and speaking actually compounds.
How that relationship gets built
Stay reachable between sessions; answer the odd follow-up question from a student who remembers your talk.
Offer a standing lighter-touch option (a remote office hour, a quick review call) between the bigger annual sessions.
Introduce the club to one other useful contact when you can — this kind of reciprocity is remembered.
Managing several such relationships without losing track
A simple log of which clubs, what was covered, and when you last spoke prevents repeating the same talk to the same audience and helps you tailor the next one.
See how I track which colleges I've spoken at.

posts.title: Fine-tuning on a laptop or a free GPU: a VRAM budget walkthrough
posts.description: Where the memory goes when you fine-tune — weights, adapters, optimiser state, activations — and the concrete settings that fit a 1–3B model into 4–6 GB of VRAM without giving up quality.
posts.text:
The most common message I get about FineTune Studio is some version of "I only have a 4 GB card, is this hopeless?". It is not. Fine-tuning a 1.7B model at about 3.2 GB of VRAM is exactly what the platform does. The trick is knowing where the memory goes and cutting the parts that do not affect quality.
Where the memory goes
Base weights — a 1.7B model in 16-bit is roughly 3.4 GB; in 4-bit it is under 1.2 GB. Quantising the frozen base is the biggest single saving.
Adapters and their optimiser state — small by design; tens of megabytes at rank 16.
Activations — grow with sequence length and batch size. This is the part you control most directly.
Framework overhead — CUDA context and caches, a few hundred megabytes you cannot avoid.
Settings that fit in 4–6 GB
4-bit base with double quantisation, adapters in bf16 or fp16.
Per-device batch of 1 with gradient accumulation of 16.
Gradient checkpointing on — slower steps, far smaller activations.
Sequence length capped at the 95th percentile of your data, not the model maximum.
A paged 8-bit optimiser so state can spill to CPU under pressure.
Free and cheap GPUs
Free notebook GPUs are enough for a first run on a small model, with two caveats: sessions end, so checkpoint to persistent storage every few hundred steps, and the disk is slow, so keep datasets small and pre-tokenised. FineTune Studio's three inference paths — local, a vLLM server, or a Hugging Face Space — exist because the machine you train on is rarely the machine you serve from.
What you give up, and what you do not
You give up speed: small batches and checkpointing make steps slower. You do not give up much quality for narrow tasks; QLoRA adapters on a quantised base track 16-bit LoRA closely. The honest way to confirm that is the base-versus-tuned comparison in how to evaluate a fine-tuned model honestly.
Hardware is a constraint, not an excuse. The students who ship fine-tuned models on borrowed GPUs learn more than the ones waiting for an A100.

posts.title: Two nights, almost no sleep: building STROT in public
posts.description: 48+ hours of system design, dashboards, pitch prep and coffee — what building in public during a hackathon actually looks like.
posts.text:
Over 48+ hours in December 2025, my team worked through system design, dashboards and flows, UI and logic, and pitch prep to bring STROT — a hackathon project aimed at breaking the cycle of generational poverty through what we called "BAL. BUDDHI. VIDYA." — to life.
What building in public actually captures
Not a demo, not a pitch — code flying, designs changing, logic breaking and getting fixed, all while the clock keeps ticking. The moments worth sharing are the grind, not the polished five-minute version of it.
The reminder that stuck
Products aren't born in slides. They're forged in late nights, debates and lines of code — and that's true whether the hackathon ends in a trophy or, as this one did, in a lesson about pitching instead.

posts.title: Saying yes to every college invite (and when I've learned to say no)
posts.description: Early on, every invite feels precious. A few criteria for declining without guilt, once speaking becomes a repeat commitment rather than a rare opportunity.
posts.text:
The first few invites feel too precious to decline. Once speaking becomes a repeat commitment rather than a rare event, saying yes to everything starts costing the quality of every session.
When declining is the right call
The date genuinely conflicts with something already committed, and rescheduling would shortchange either.
The audience or format is a poor fit for what you actually do well — better to recommend someone else than deliver a mismatched session.
You're already stretched that week and would show up under-prepared, which serves nobody.
How to decline without burning the relationship
Respond quickly, say yes to a future date if one's genuinely open, and where possible suggest someone else who'd fit well. Organisers remember a gracious no far better than a rushed, mediocre yes.
See speaking at multiple events in one month without burning out.

posts.title: GenAI engineer interview questions I'd ask (with what a good answer sounds like)
posts.description: Twenty questions across RAG, fine-tuning, evaluation, reliability and product judgement that separate candidates who built systems from candidates who read about them — with the shape of a strong answer for each.
posts.text:
When I review candidates for AI work at SCULT INDIA or coach students before interviews, the questions that matter are the ones a tutorial cannot answer for you. Here are the ones I would ask, grouped, with what a strong answer contains. Prepare these and you will also have built the right things.
Retrieval
How did you decide your chunk size? Strong: an evaluation set and recall numbers at three sizes.
Why hybrid retrieval? Strong: an example query where vectors failed and keywords worked.
What does your system do when nothing relevant is retrieved? Strong: a threshold and a refusal, tuned on unanswerable questions.
How do you know your citations are correct? Strong: markers resolved to chunks, a faithfulness check.
Fine-tuning
When would you fine-tune instead of using retrieval? Strong: behaviour versus knowledge, with an example of each.
What did your loss curve look like, and when did you stop? Strong: eval loss, checkpoints, the best step.
How did you prove the tuned model was better? Strong: base versus tuned on held-out data, same rubric.
What was wrong with your dataset the first time? Everyone has an answer; the honest one is the strong one.
Reliability and cost
What happens when the provider is down? Strong: fallback, retries with limits, a typed error to the client.
How do you control cost per request? Strong: context caps, caching, cheaper routing for simple cases.
What do you log for an LLM call? Strong: request id, model, tokens, latency, retrieval scores — never raw personal data.
How would you test this system in CI? Strong: golden prompts, schema checks, an evaluation script with thresholds.
Product judgement
Was AI the right tool for this feature? Strong: names the part done with plain code.
What did you cut, and why? Strong: a deliberate scope decision.
Who used it, and what did they say? Strong: named users and a change made because of them.
Where does user data go? Strong: a one-sentence data flow, and what is never stored.
About you
Show me something running. The best candidates have a URL ready.
Walk me through the hardest bug. Reveals who built what.
What would you build differently now? Reveals reflection.
What are you learning this month? Reveals momentum.
Notice that every strong answer is evidence from something you built. That is the whole strategy: build the projects in the roadmap, and the interview prepares itself.

posts.title: Guest of honour at a college fest: what the role actually involves beyond a ribbon-cutting
posts.description: A guest-of-honour slot is often assumed to be ceremonial. Done well, it's a short talk, real interaction with students, and a few photos that matter to the organisers.
posts.text:
A 'guest of honour' invite sounds purely ceremonial — arrive, get garlanded, leave. Done well, the role is closer to a short, high-energy guest speaking slot with extra visibility.
What the role actually needs
A short, upbeat address (10-15 minutes) that respects the ceremonial format but still gives students one real, usable idea.
Genuine time on the floor afterward — walking the exhibits, talking to a few teams, not just sitting on stage.
Willingness to be in photos with students and organisers; this is often the actual reason a fest wants a guest of honour, and it's a fair trade for the platform they're giving you.
Making the ceremonial version worth it anyway
Ask the organisers beforehand if you can also run a short breakout session later in the day — many fests welcome this, and it turns a purely ceremonial slot into a real teaching opportunity too.
See speaking topics I offer colleges for formats that adapt well to this dual role.

posts.title: How to read a loss curve during fine-tuning (and when to stop)
posts.description: What training and evaluation loss actually tell you, the curve shapes that mean overfitting, a learning rate problem or a broken dataset, and why live telemetry beats reading logs afterwards.
posts.text:
