RAG.NextUpgrad ships with automatic multi-provider fallback because the first client demo I ever gave hit a provider outage — and I never wanted to explain that again.
The abstraction that makes it possible
Put every provider behind one interface: generate(messages, options) → stream of tokens plus usage. Keep prompts in a neutral chat format and translate to each provider's schema inside the adapter. The moment a prompt depends on one vendor's special syntax, fallback silently degrades quality.
Deciding when to fall back
Hard failures — connection errors, 5xx, authentication errors — fall back immediately.
Rate limits — retry once with backoff, then fall back; a queue of retries during an outage is a slow outage.
Timeouts before the first token — fall back; after the first token, finish or fail cleanly rather than restarting with a different voice mid-answer.
Content refusals — do not fall back automatically. A refusal is a signal, not an error.
Ordering providers
Order by quality for your evaluation set, then by cost. Keep a cheap, fast model as the last resort so the product degrades to "shorter, plainer answers" rather than "no answers". Record which provider answered each request; without that field you cannot debug a quality complaint.
What fallback cannot fix
Bad retrieval — if the context is wrong, every provider will be wrong with confidence. Fix that with a confidence gate.
Provider-specific behaviour your product relies on, such as a JSON mode or a tool-calling format. Test every provider against your schema.
Cost surprises — a fallback to a pricier model during a long outage can double a month's bill. Cap fallback spend.
Choosing a primary provider deserves its own framework — I wrote one in choosing an LLM provider. Whatever you choose first, design so that the choice is reversible at runtime.

posts.title: How many teams can one judge fairly see in a day? The number organisers underestimate
posts.description: Judging quality drops sharply after a certain number of pitches in a day. A realistic per-judge cap and how to schedule around it.
posts.text:
Organisers often schedule one judge for thirty teams in a day because the math of judges-available divided by teams-total made that number convenient. Judging quality does not survive thirty pitches in a day.
A realistic cap
Somewhere around twelve to fifteen substantive pitches (five minutes plus Q&A) is where a judge's attention and written feedback quality start degrading noticeably. Past that, scores compress toward the middle and feedback gets generic.
Build in real breaks between blocks of five or six pitches, not just a lunch break in the middle of the day.
If team count exceeds what your judge panel can fairly see, add judges or run a first-round screening with a lighter rubric before the full panel sees finalists.
Ask judges directly, before the event, how many they're comfortable doing — don't just divide teams by headcount.
See inviting a hackathon judge: what organisers should send for getting this number right from the first email.

posts.title: The ten questions students ask me most (and my honest answers)
posts.description: The questions that come up after every campus session — on DSA versus projects, which language, hackathons, certificates, startups versus jobs, and whether it is too late — with the answers a mentor actually gives.
posts.text:
After every talk the same ten questions arrive, at the podium and in messages for the following week. Here they are with the answers I give — short, because the students who ask them need a direction, not a lecture.
The questions
DSA or projects? Both, but projects first if you have to choose in Year 1. A shipped project makes DSA practice meaningful and gets you into rooms where it is tested.
Which language? Python for AI, JavaScript or TypeScript for the web. Pick one, build three things, then learn the other. The language matters less than finishing.
Is a non-IIT college a disadvantage? For campus placements, sometimes. For everything else — hackathons, open source, remote roles, startups — the internet does not check your college. I studied computer applications at VSICS in India; the wins came from showing up at IIT Roorkee and CSJMU with working projects.
Are certificates worth it? Only as a study structure. Recruiters look at projects; see portfolio over certificates.
How do I get into hackathons with no experience? Join a team as the person who does research, testing and the pitch; see your first hackathon as a first-year.
Startup or job? Job first unless you already have users. Three of us started SCULT INDIA while studying, but with paying clients, not a pitch deck.
How do I get noticed? Publish what you build — GitHub, LinkedIn, a small blog. The people who invite you to speak or judge found you because you posted.
Is it too late to start in Year 3? No. A focused year of building beats three years of intending to.
Which AI area should I pick? Do one RAG project, one fine-tuning project and one vision or speech project. Pick the one you did not want to stop working on.
Will AI take our jobs? It will take the jobs of people who refuse to use it. Learn to build with it, and you become the person deciding what it does.
The question nobody asks aloud
"Am I good enough?" The honest answer is that nobody in the room knows yet, including me, and the only way to find out is to ship something and show it to someone. That is what mentors are for, and it is why I keep answering these ten.

posts.title: 25 AI hackathon project ideas for 2026 (with the hard part of each)
posts.description: Project ideas across agriculture, education, health, accessibility, campus life and small business — each with the one hard problem that makes it worth a judge's attention.
posts.text:
The idea matters less than teams think and more than they act like. A judge does not reward novelty for its own sake; a judge rewards a real problem with a demonstrable solution. These ideas are chosen because each has a clear user and one genuinely hard part — the part that will impress if you solve it.
Agriculture and rural
Voice-first crop advisory in a regional language — hard part: evaluation without benchmarks. (Krishi Gyan, our Changethon winner, lived here.)
Mandi price alerts from noisy public data — hard part: data cleaning.
Pest identification from a phone photo with a confidence gate — hard part: refusing when unsure.
Education and campus
Syllabus-grounded study assistant with page citations — hard part: retrieval quality.
Lecture-to-notes with slide alignment — hard part: alignment.
Timetable and room-clash resolver for departments — hard part: constraints, not AI.
Notice-board reader for visually impaired students — hard part: skewed, handwritten text.
Placement-prep interviewer that grades against a rubric — hard part: consistent grading.
Health and wellbeing
Medication reminder that reads prescriptions — hard part: extraction accuracy and safety.
Symptom-to-department triage for a college clinic — hard part: knowing when to escalate to a human.
Mental-health check-in with strict escalation rules — hard part: the rules, not the chat.
Food, community and NGOs
Real-time surplus food matching between donors, NGOs and volunteers — hard part: logistics. (Annapurna won BYTEBATTLE with this.)
Volunteer shift scheduler with fairness constraints — hard part: fairness.
Donation receipt extraction and reporting for small NGOs — hard part: schema validation.
Small business
Invoice checker that validates totals and flags anomalies — hard part: deterministic scoring.
WhatsApp order-taker for a local shop — hard part: ambiguity in orders.
Product photo to catalogue listing with honest descriptions — hard part: not inventing specs.
Review summariser that cites the review it summarises — hard part: faithfulness.
Accessibility and civic
Sign-language-to-text for common phrases — hard part: dataset.
Form-filling assistant for government schemes — hard part: eligibility logic.
Bus arrival predictor from crowd-sourced pings — hard part: sparse data.
Complaint router for a municipal helpline — hard part: classification with accountability.

posts.title: Judging a remote hackathon vs an on-site one: what actually changes
posts.description: A demo over a video call fails differently than one in a room. What a judge needs to adjust for a remote hackathon, and what stays exactly the same.
posts.text:
Judging remotely changes the mechanics of a demo far more than it changes the rubric — the criteria stay the same, but what can go wrong shifts entirely.
What changes
Screen-share lag and connection drops mean a team should have a backup recording ready, and a judge should ask for one before it's needed.
Reading a room's energy is gone; judges have to ask more directly whether a team is nervous or genuinely stuck, since body language cues are limited.
Time zones matter for scheduling pitch slots fairly if teams or judges are spread across regions.
What stays exactly the same
The rubric, the requirement that a demo runs on a live input, and the expectation of written feedback for every team don't change just because the room is virtual. Remote is a logistics difference, not a standards difference.
See mentoring a hackathon team remotely for the same distinction from the mentor's side.

posts.title: Mentoring a hackathon team remotely: what works over a call
posts.description: How to mentor student teams you cannot sit beside: three fixed check-ins, screen-share rules, a shared scoping doc, and how to run a mock pitch over video.
posts.text:
Most of the teams I mentor before hackathons are in other cities, so the mentoring happens over calls squeezed between their build sprints. Remote mentoring fails when it is unstructured; it works when the team knows exactly when the mentor appears and what to bring.
Three fixed check-ins
Scoping call, before the event or in hour one. Twenty minutes. Output: one sentence for the problem, one for the user, one for the demo path, roles written down. I ask the scoping question until the team can answer it.
Midpoint call. Fifteen minutes of screen-share on the walking skeleton. I look for a real end-to-end path, however ugly, and for anything being built that is not on the demo path.
Mock pitch, two hours before freeze. The full three minutes with a timer, then Q&A using the questions judges ask, then one strength and one fix.
Rules that make calls useful
The team shares their screen, not their slides. I want to see the running thing.
One person talks per topic — the person who built it.
Questions between calls go in one shared document with context, not as a stream of messages. I answer in batches.
I do not write code. I point, ask and suggest. The learning stays with the team, and the rules stay intact.
The shared scoping doc
One page: problem, user, demo path, roles, checkpoints, what has been cut. The team updates it; I read it before every call. It is the single most effective tool for remote mentoring because it forces decisions into writing.
For organisers
Remote mentors work well when the schedule publishes their slots and teams can book them. Assign two or three teams per mentor at most. I mentor and judge remotely for student hackathons anywhere in India; write to pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or see the invite page.

posts.title: Streaming LLM answers with FastAPI and Server-Sent Events
posts.description: How to stream tokens from an LLM to a browser with FastAPI and SSE: the endpoint shape, the client, error handling mid-stream, and the pitfalls with proxies and timeouts.
posts.text:
A ten-second wait followed by a wall of text feels broken. The same answer streamed word by word feels fast, even when total time is identical. Every AI product I ship streams, and Server-Sent Events over FastAPI is the simplest way to do it.
Why SSE over WebSockets
Token streaming is one-directional: the server talks, the client listens. SSE is plain HTTP, works through most proxies, reconnects automatically in the browser, and needs no upgrade handshake. WebSockets earn their complexity when the client also streams — live speech-to-text is the case where I use them instead.
The endpoint shape
Accept the question and any document scope as a POST, validate, and run retrieval before opening the stream — retrieval errors should return a normal HTTP error, not a broken stream.
Return a StreamingResponse with media type text/event-stream and an async generator that yields events.
Send a first event carrying metadata: the citation map, the retrieval confidence, and a request id.
Yield token events as the provider streams them; end with a done event that includes usage and timing.
Handling failure mid-stream
Once headers are sent you cannot change the status code, so errors must travel inside the stream as a typed event. RAG.NextUpgrad's multi-provider fallback works at this layer: if the primary provider fails before the first token, the generator switches providers and the client never notices; if it fails mid-answer, the client receives an error event and a retry hint rather than a truncated paragraph.
Pitfalls
Reverse proxies buffering the response — disable buffering for the stream route and send a comment line every few seconds as a heartbeat.
Idle timeouts on free hosts — heartbeats also keep the connection alive during a slow reranking pass.
Forgetting to flush — yield small strings; do not accumulate.
Client-side, use fetch with a reader rather than EventSource if you need POST bodies; EventSource only supports GET.
Streaming is a small amount of code with an outsized effect on how a product feels. It is also the first thing I demo to students who think an AI app is just an API call and a text box.

posts.title: Five mistakes every first-time hackathon judge makes (I made most of them too)
posts.description: Scoring on charisma, comparing teams instead of scoring against the rubric, and other first-time-judge mistakes — and the simple fixes for each.
posts.text:
First-time judges make a predictable set of mistakes, mostly from applying instinct instead of the rubric they were handed.
The five
Scoring on charisma: a confident presenter with a thin project outscores a nervous one with a strong build, unless you deliberately correct for it.
Comparing teams to each other in the moment instead of scoring each against the rubric independently, which drifts as the day goes on.
Letting the first team anchor the scale — team one gets a 9, and every later team gets judged relative to them instead of the criteria.
Asking softball questions instead of the one question that tests whether the team actually understands their own project.
Writing no notes, then trying to reconstruct feedback from memory at the end of a long day of pitches.
The fix for all five
Score immediately after each pitch, against the written rubric, with one sentence of notes — before the next team starts. It sounds small; it's the single habit that prevents most of this.
See how judges should give feedback.

posts.title: How I prepare a 45-minute campus talk
posts.description: The preparation behind a talk students remember: one question the talk answers, a story with a failure in it, a live demo, three rehearsals with a timer, and the one thing I ask coordinators before I write a slide.
posts.text:
The talks that went well — the VSICS induction, the AI mentorship session — were not the ones with the best slides. They were the ones I had prepared around a single question the room actually had. Here is the process, so speakers can borrow it and coordinators can see what a prepared speaker needs from them.
Ask the coordinator one thing
"What do these students worry about right now?" First-years worry about being behind. Final-years worry about placements. A club worries about whether their projects are good enough. The talk is the answer to that worry, and everything that does not serve the answer is cut.
One question, one story, one demo
The question the talk answers, written at the top of my notes. For the induction: "What should I do in the next three years?"
A story with a failure in it. Living Space Automation failing before anything shipped; STROT losing after two sleepless nights. Students trust a speaker who has lost.
A live demo, even in a talk. Ninety seconds of a real system running does what ten slides of architecture cannot.
Structure
Open with the worry, not with my bio. Answer it in the first five minutes, then spend the rest earning the answer with evidence. End with a task for this week and a way to reach me. Slides are sparse: one idea each, a photo or a number, no paragraphs.
Rehearse three times, with a timer
Once alone to find the shape, once recorded to hear the filler, once to a friend who will be honest. A 45-minute slot means 38 minutes of talk; venues eat the difference. If I cannot finish early in rehearsal, I cut a section, never speed up.
On the day
Arrive early; test the projector with my laptop; learn the host's name and six students' names before starting.
Stand where I can see faces. Move when a section changes.
Stop on time. Questions run as long as students want.
Preparation is mostly subtraction. The talk students remember is the one that answered their question and left before they were tired.

posts.title: A hackathon pitch deck template that fits in three minutes
posts.description: Seven slides, thirty seconds each, in the order judges need to hear them — with what to say on each, what to cut, and how to hand off to the live demo without losing the room.
posts.text:
The pitch that won Product Genesis at CSJMU was delivered to a Vice Chancellor in front of a full hall; the one that lost with STROT was delivered to a panel of three. The difference was not the idea. It was whether the first minute made the judges want the second. This template is what I coach teams toward now.
The seven slides
The person and the pain — one human, one situation, what goes wrong today. No logo, no team names yet.
Why now, why us — one line on why this problem is tractable this weekend and what your team knows about it.
What we built — one sentence, then hand off to the live demo. This slide is a doorway, not a description.
Live demo — ninety seconds, real input, one path. See the demo that works live.
How it works — one diagram, three boxes, the one technical decision you are proud of.
What we cut and why — the honesty slide. Judges score it higher than any feature list.
What happens Monday — the next step if this continued, and what you would need.
What to cut
The team introduction slide. Names go in the footer; the judge will meet you in Q&A.
The market-size slide with a number from a report you did not read.
The full architecture diagram. Three boxes, not thirteen.
Any slide that starts with "In today's world".
Delivery
One speaker for the story, one for the demo, then everyone answers questions about their own part. Rehearse with a timer until you finish at 2:40, because the venue will cost you twenty seconds. I covered the two-minute version in how to pitch a startup idea in two minutes.
A pitch deck is a script for the judge's attention. Spend it on the problem and the demo; everything else is footnotes.

posts.title: Mentorship session, workshop or talk: pick the right format for your students
posts.description: A guide for coordinators choosing between a guest talk, a hands-on workshop and a mentorship session — what each achieves, how long it needs, who should attend, and how to combine them.
posts.text:
Coordinators usually ask for "a session on AI". That single word hides three different events with different outcomes, and picking the wrong one is why students file out of good talks having learned nothing they can use. Here is how I help colleges choose.
The guest talk
45 to 60 minutes, any room size, one speaker, questions at the end. It changes what students believe is possible — a practitioner from a similar college describing what they shipped does more for ambition than any poster. It does not change what students can do. Book it for inductions, fests and department days.
The workshop
90 minutes to a full day, 30 to 80 students, laptops, a live build and hands-on blocks. It changes what students can do by the end of the day — everyone leaves with something running. It needs Wi-Fi, tables and a coordinator who has confirmed prerequisites. Book it when a club or a batch is ready to build.
The mentorship session
60 to 90 minutes, 10 to 40 students, conversational, built around their projects and questions rather than a fixed syllabus. It changes decisions — which project to pursue, which hackathon to enter, what to do in Year 2. The AI Mentorship Session at VSICS in April 2025 mixed this with a showcase of a hackathon-winning project, which is a strong combination.
Choose by outcome
Students should believe they can → talk.
Students should be able to → workshop.
Students should decide → mentorship session.
Combine them
The format that works best on a single campus visit: a 40-minute talk for the whole batch in the morning, a 90-minute workshop for the club in the afternoon, and a mentorship hour for the students who stayed. One visit, three outcomes. Coordinators can find the logistics in how to invite a GenAI guest speaker, and the formats I offer on the invite page.

posts.title: Innovation vs execution: how I actually weigh a hackathon rubric's criteria
posts.description: Most rubrics list innovation, execution, impact and presentation with no guidance on relative weight. A concrete weighting scheme and the reasoning behind it.
posts.text:
A rubric that lists innovation, execution, impact and presentation without weights leaves every judge silently applying their own — which is exactly the inconsistency a rubric is supposed to prevent.
A weighting I use and explain to teams upfront
Execution, 35%: does the demo actually run on an input the team didn't rehearse.
Problem clarity and impact, 30%: is there a real person with a real problem behind this, not just a technology showcase.
Innovation, 20%: a genuinely new angle, not necessarily a new technology — a clever use of an existing one counts.
Presentation, 15%: clear communication, not production value — a plain, honest pitch should never lose to a polished, vague one.
Why execution outweighs innovation
A brilliant idea that doesn't run teaches a judge nothing about the team's engineering; a working, unglamorous solution teaches a lot. Weight rewards what you actually want the competition to select for.
See judging AI hackathon projects: what to check for how execution gets verified in practice.

posts.title: Citations in RAG answers: how to make every sentence traceable to a source
posts.description: Design patterns for citation-grounded answers: chunk identifiers, inline markers, page references, and how to verify that a citation actually supports the claim it is attached to.
posts.text:
An answer without a source is an opinion with good grammar. The reason RAG.NextUpgrad streams citation-grounded answers is not decoration; it is what lets a user check the system in ten seconds instead of trusting it blindly. Citations are the difference between a demo and a tool people rely on.
Give every chunk a stable identity
At ingest, assign each chunk an identifier that encodes document, page and position. The prompt presents chunks with these identifiers, and the model is instructed to reference them inline. Because the identifiers are yours, you can resolve a marker back to a document title, a page number and the exact passage — and render it as a clickable citation.
Inline markers beat a footer list
A list of sources at the bottom tells the reader something was used, not what. Sentence-level markers — "the limit is five requests per second [2]" — attach each claim to its evidence. The OCR & Speech Workspace uses page-level citations for scanned books, which is what makes a 400-page PDF usable: the reader jumps to page 214 rather than searching.
Verify the citations, not just the answer
Check that every marker resolves to a chunk that was actually in the prompt. Models occasionally invent [7] when only five chunks existed.
Check that the cited chunk supports the sentence it is attached to — an entailment pass, by rubric or by a judge model.
Strip any sentence that has no supporting chunk, or flag it visibly. Silent unsupported sentences are how trust erodes.
Streaming and citations together
Streaming complicates citations because markers arrive mid-sentence. The pattern that works: stream the text as it comes, resolve markers client-side against a citation map sent before the first token, and render the source panel progressively. Users get speed and traceability at once.
If you are building a RAG project for a portfolio, citations are the feature that makes a reviewer lean forward. They show you understand that the model is a writer, and the documents are the authority.

posts.title: Running a remote guest lecture that doesn't feel remote
posts.description: How to deliver a guest lecture over video to a college classroom: the room setup on their side, the camera and audio on yours, interaction every ten minutes, and a co-host who owns the chat.
posts.text:
A remote guest lecture is usually a face on a projector talking to a silent room. It does not have to be. Some of my most engaged sessions have been remote — for colleges in other states that could not host a visit — because remote forces a discipline that in-person lets you skip. Here is what works from both sides of the link.
On the college's side
A camera pointed at the students, not just at the screen. The speaker needs to see the room.
One good microphone passed to whoever speaks; laptop mics from the back row are inaudible.
A co-host — a student or faculty member — who owns the chat, relays questions and manages the hands-on block.
The session link tested from the actual room an hour before.
On the speaker's side
Camera at eye level, face lit from the front, a plain background.
Two screens: one shared, one for the room camera and chat.
Sharing a window, not the whole screen, with font size at 20 or larger.
A wired connection and a phone hotspot as a fallback.
Interaction every ten minutes
Remote attention decays faster. Ask for a show of hands on camera, a one-word answer in the chat, a vote between two options. In the hands-on block, students paste their output into the chat and you read three aloud. The session format works remotely if the interaction points are kept.
Questions
Collect them in the chat throughout; the co-host groups and reads them. Take questions on camera from the room too — a student walking to the microphone is a moment the room remembers. Leave twenty minutes; remote audiences ask more once the first person breaks the ice.
Afterwards
Send the recording, the code and one task within an hour. Remote sessions fade faster from memory; the follow-up is what makes them stick. I deliver most of my out-of-state sessions this way; colleges anywhere in India can book one through the invite page.

posts.title: Panel judging vs solo judging: why a hackathon needs more than one judge in the room
posts.description: A single judge's taste becomes the whole competition's outcome. A panel with a shared rubric and a calibration round fixes that — here's how the two formats actually differ.
posts.text:
A single judge's personal taste — a preference for slick UI over hard engineering, say — becomes the entire competition's outcome when there's only one scorer. A panel exists specifically to average that out.
What a panel needs to actually work
A shared rubric with weighted criteria, agreed before the first pitch, not improvised per team.
A calibration round: score one or two teams together as a panel and discuss the gap before scoring independently.
An odd number of judges per team where possible, so ties resolve without a forced tiebreaker rule.
When solo judging is actually fine
A small, low-stakes internal hackathon with a handful of teams can work with one judge if everyone agrees the exercise is more about feedback than ranking. The moment prizes or resume-worthy results are on the line, a panel is worth the extra coordination.
See what a judges' briefing should cover for how to run the calibration round in practice.

posts.title: A 36-hour hackathon timeline, hour by hour
posts.description: A realistic schedule from problem selection to judging — with the two checkpoints that separate finished projects from ambitious fragments, and where to sleep.
posts.text:
Two nights, almost no sleep — that was STROT, and we did not win. The projects that won for us followed a plan. This is the timeline I share with teams I mentor, built for a 36-hour event with judging at hour 36.
Hours 0–2: decide
Problem, user, one demo path, roles on paper (see forming a hackathon team). Talk to three people who have the problem if you possibly can — organisers, volunteers, the canteen staff. Do not open an editor yet.
Hours 2–6: skeleton
Repository, deployment target, a page that loads, an API that returns a hard-coded answer, the AI call working once. Everything wired end-to-end with fake data. This is the walking skeleton, and it is your first checkpoint.
Hours 6–14: the core feature
Replace the fake data with the real thing along the single demo path. Storyteller drafts the pitch and slides in parallel and interviews the team for the story. Sleep in shifts if the event runs overnight; the 3 a.m. code is the code you rewrite at 9.
Hours 14–24: make it real
Seeded data, error handling on the demo path, the one alternate path, a landing screen that explains the problem. First full rehearsal of the pitch with a timer at hour 22. Cut anything that is not on the demo path.
Hours 24–30: polish and rehearse
Rehearse the pitch five times. Fix the front end where judges will look. Prepare answers to the five likely questions (see questions judges ask in hackathon Q&A). Record the fallback video.
Hours 30–34: freeze
No new features. Run the demo checklist. Charge everything. Eat.
Hours 34–36: present
Arrive early, test the projector, breathe. Let the storyteller open, the builder demo, and whoever built each part answer for it.
The two checkpoints — skeleton at hour 6, freeze at hour 30 — are the whole method. Teams that hit both almost always have something real to show; teams that skip them present a plan.

posts.title: From campus to community: the TechVerse Enclave playbook
posts.description: How a college group became a 500+ member developer community: the first thirty members, the weekly rhythm, admins who own areas, sessions that convert lurkers, and what nearly killed it.
posts.text:
TechVerse Enclave grew out of a few students at VSICS helping each other ship and became a community of 500+ members across AI, web, cybersecurity, data and startups, with a LinkedIn community launched in September 2025 and 200+ students mentored along the way. None of that was luck; most of it was rhythm. This is the playbook, for anyone trying to do the same at their college.
Start with thirty, not three hundred
The first thirty members set the culture. We recruited people who had built something — anything — and asked them to post it. A community where the first thing you see is someone's project becomes a community where people post projects. One where the first thing you see is a motivational quote becomes a feed.
A weekly rhythm people can predict
One session a week, same day, same time — a build, a talk or a review.
One thread a week asking what people shipped, with admins answering every reply.
One external event a month: a hackathon to enter as teams, a speaker, a visit.
Admins who own areas
Six admins — Raman Shukla, Saksham Gupta, Nikhil Tiwari, Bidhan Bhattacharya, Om Tripathi and me — each owning a track: AI, web, cybersecurity, data, startups, operations. Ownership means the track has a session calendar and a person to ask. Shared ownership means nobody owns it.
Sessions that convert lurkers
Ninety percent of any community watches. The sessions that pulled people into participating were the ones with a hands-on block and a show-and-tell — the format in a tech club session format that works. Someone who has shown their work once on a projector posts it online the next week.
What nearly killed it
Growing membership faster than sessions. Numbers without rhythm produce silence.
Admin burnout around exams. The fix was a published calendar with owners, so a missed week was a known gap rather than a slow death.
Letting the channel become announcements only. Communities die quietly when members stop replying to each other.
What it made possible
Hackathon teams that already knew how to work together — Team TechVerse won three first prizes in 2025 — and a pipeline of students ready for the mentorship sessions we ran on campus. If you are starting a community at your college and want a session to kick it off, I do those; see how to start a tech community on your campus and the invite page.

posts.title: How to become a hackathon judge: what actually gets you invited to the panel
posts.description: Organisers don't search a directory for judges — they ask people they already trust. What builds that trust before the first invitation ever arrives.
posts.text:
Nobody becomes a hackathon judge by applying to a listing — organisers ask someone whose judgement they already trust, usually because of something public: a rubric they published, a talk they gave, projects they've clearly evaluated before.
What actually builds that trust
A published, reusable rubric — see a hackathon judging rubric organisers can copy — that shows you think about scoring before anyone asks you to.
Mentoring at hackathons first; mentors who give sharp, structured feedback are the pool organisers pull judges from.
Being visibly active in the student-hackathon community — organising, speaking, writing — so your name is the one that comes up.
Making yourself easy to invite
Put a standing offer somewhere organisers can find it, with the logistics already answered: on-site or remote, what you need in a briefing, how many teams you can fairly assess. I keep mine on the invite page for exactly this reason.
See what hackathon judges look for for the method itself once you're on a panel.

posts.title: Choosing an embedding model for RAG (and when to switch)
posts.description: How embedding models differ, what to test before committing, why multilingual matters in India, and how to swap models later without re-architecting the pipeline.
posts.text:
The embedding model decides what "similar" means in your retriever. Swap it and the same query returns different chunks. Yet most projects pick one from a tutorial and never revisit it. Here is how I choose, and how I keep the option to change later.
What actually differs between models
Dimension — 384 versus 1024 dimensions changes index size and search cost more than it changes quality on small corpora.
Context length — a model that truncates at 512 tokens silently ignores the end of long chunks. Match chunk size to the model.
Domain — general web models handle policy PDFs well; code and legal text benefit from models trained on them.
Language — Hindi and Hinglish queries against English documents need a multilingual model, or you will watch retrieval fail on your own users.
Hosting — an API model is simplest; a local model keeps documents on your server, which some clients require.
Test before you commit
Take the evaluation set from how to evaluate a RAG system and index the corpus with two or three candidate models. Compare recall@5 and the rank of the correct passage. Differences are often smaller than tutorials suggest — and when they are small, pick the cheaper, faster or more private model.
Design for switching
Store the model name and dimension alongside each index, keep the embedding call behind one function, and make re-indexing a command rather than a migration. RAG.NextUpgrad's multi-provider fallback exists for generation, but the same discipline applies to embeddings: never let a single vendor's model become load-bearing for your architecture.
When to switch
Switch when recall on your own questions is the bottleneck and hybrid search plus reranking have already been added — not because a leaderboard changed. Leaderboards measure someone else's queries.

posts.title: Talks I offer colleges: RAG, fine-tuning, shipping AI, hackathons and careers
posts.description: Pranjul Rathour's current talk and workshop menu for colleges and student communities, with the audience, duration and takeaway for each — from a 40-minute induction talk to a full-day GenAI build.
posts.text:
Coordinators ask what I can speak about, so here is the menu as it stands, with what each session is for. Every talk is built from things I have shipped, won or lost, and every workshop ends with students running something they built. All of these can be on-site anywhere in India or remote.
Talks (40–60 minutes)
From college hackathons to production AI — the roadmap I gave 100+ first-years at the VSICS induction, extended: Year 1 foundations, Year 2 hackathons and internships, Year 3 placements or a startup. For inductions and fests.
What I learned winning three hackathons and losing one — Changethon at IIT Roorkee, Product Genesis at CSJMU, BYTEBATTLE, and STROT; the pitch, the demo, the team. For hackathon kick-offs.
Production RAG that refuses to hallucinate — hybrid retrieval, reranking, confidence gates and citations, from building RAG.NextUpgrad. For CS and AI batches.
Shipping AI as a small team — five production AI apps in a year, and what a 14-member student-led team gets right and wrong. For entrepreneurship cells.
AI for everyone else — an honest AI literacy session for non-CS departments; see an AI awareness session for non-CS students.
Workshops (90 minutes to a full day)
Build a RAG app from scratch — the one-day GenAI workshop syllabus; 90-minute and half-day versions available.
Fine-tune a small model on a free GPU — QLoRA end to end with an honest base-versus-tuned evaluation, based on FineTune Studio.
Ship it — FastAPI, Next.js, Docker, logs and a deploy, in one afternoon.
Mentoring and judging
Mentorship sessions built around students' own projects and decisions.
Hackathon judging with a published rubric and written feedback for every team, and hackathon mentoring before or during events.
Portfolio and mock-interview clinics for placement cells.
Logistics
Sessions for student communities are free; on-site visits ask for travel. I need the students' year and prior knowledge a week ahead, and a tested projector on the day. Everything else — past sessions, photographs, the invitation checklist — is on the campus invite page, and the email is pranjulrathour41@gmail.com.

posts.title: From a college project to a startup: what actually changes, beyond the pitch deck
posts.description: Turning a hackathon project into a real startup changes the constraints far more than it changes the code. What founders wish they'd known first.
posts.text:
A college project has one user (you, or your team) and no deadline pressure beyond a demo date. A startup version of the same idea has real users, real support requests, and a cost structure that suddenly matters.
What actually changes
Reliability now has a cost attached — a bug that was funny in a demo is a support ticket and a refund request in production.
Cost control stops being optional — a college project's API bill was probably a rounding error; a startup's is a line item someone has to justify.
You need at least one other person who can operate the system when you're unavailable — a hackathon project only ever needed you.
What genuinely doesn't change
The core technical judgement — knowing when to use RAG versus fine-tuning, how to evaluate honestly, how to keep a system debuggable — transfers directly. The hard part of the transition is operational discipline, not new technical knowledge.
See how to pitch a startup idea in two minutes and from an engineering student to GenAI engineer.

posts.title: Forming a hackathon team: roles, skills and the mistake most teams make
posts.description: How to assemble a team that finishes: the four roles that matter, why five friends with the same skill lose, how to split work in the first hour, and what mentors notice about team dynamics.
posts.text:
Team TechVerse — Raman Shukla, Saksham Gupta and me — won three first prizes in 2025 not because we were the strongest coders in the room, but because we had stopped overlapping. When I mentor teams before a hackathon, formation is the first thing I fix.
The four roles
Builder — owns the core feature and the demo path. Usually backend or the AI piece.
Interface — owns what the judge sees: the front end, the flow, the seeded data.
Storyteller — owns the problem statement, the pitch, the slides and the Q&A plan; also does user research in hour one.
Integrator — keeps the pieces working together, manages the repo, runs the demo rehearsals. In a team of three, the builder or interface person takes this.
The mistake
Five friends who all write React. Everyone builds screens, nobody owns the problem, and the pitch is written at 4 a.m. by whoever is still awake. Mixed skills beat matched skills; a team with one strong coder and one strong communicator will outperform four coders.
The first hour
Pick the problem and the user, in one sentence, on paper.
Define the single demo path you will show; everything else is optional.
Assign roles explicitly and write them on the same paper.
Set two checkpoints — a walking skeleton at the one-third mark, a frozen demo two hours before judging.
What mentors and judges notice
Whether the person answering a question built the thing they are answering about. Whether the team disagrees productively or defers to one loud voice. Whether someone can say "we cut that on purpose". Team dynamics are visible from across the room, and they predict whether the project survives the weekend.
Form the team for the problem, not for friendship. You can still be friends afterwards — especially if you win.

posts.title: A tech club session format that keeps 60 students engaged for 90 minutes
posts.description: The session structure Pranjul Rathour uses for campus workshops: a live build in front of the room, a fifteen-minute hands-on block, a show-and-tell, and the three rules that stop a workshop becoming a lecture.
posts.text:
The AI Mentorship Session at VSICS in April 2025 ran for a seminar hall of students and ended with people staying back to ask questions — not because the topic was new, but because the format never let attention drop. Here is the structure, minute by minute, for any tech club or coordinator planning a session.
The 90-minute shape
0–10: the problem, not the agenda. Open with a real situation the room recognises — a project that failed, a demo that broke — and the question the session will answer.
10–40: build it live. Code in front of the room, narrating decisions. Make a mistake on purpose and fix it; the recovery teaches more than the plan.
40–55: hands-on block. One small task everyone does on their own laptop or phone, with a visible target. Walk the room.
55–70: show-and-tell. Three volunteers show their result on the projector. Praise specifics; fix one thing each.
70–85: the map. Now, and only now, the slides: where this fits, what to learn next, one resource.
85–90: the ask. One concrete thing to do this week, and how to reach you.
Three rules
No slide before minute 70. If it can be shown, show it.
Every fifteen minutes the room does something: answers a question, votes, types.
Names. Learn six in the first ten minutes and use them.
Logistics that decide the session
Wi-Fi tested with sixty devices, not one. A hotspot as backup. The projector checked with the actual laptop. Font size at 20 or larger. A shared document with the code and links posted before the session, not after. These decide more sessions than the content does.
For coordinators
Book a room with tables, not an auditorium, for anything hands-on. Cap it at 60 to 80. Tell the speaker the students' year and what they already know. I have written the full checklist in how to invite a GenAI guest speaker to your college.

posts.title: Time management for CS students trying to ship projects and pass exams at the same time
posts.description: Side projects and coursework compete for the same hours. A realistic weekly structure that protects both instead of sacrificing one for the other.
posts.text:
Students building a portfolio while carrying a full course load usually end up sacrificing one entirely during exam weeks, then feeling behind on the other for the rest of the semester.
A structure that protects both
Fixed, small side-project time (even 45 minutes, most days) beats occasional long weekend binges that never survive exam season.
Batch project work into short, well-defined milestones — 'ship the retrieval step this week' — rather than an open-ended 'work on the project'.
During exam weeks, explicitly pause the project rather than half-attending to both; a clean pause is easier to resume than a project left in a broken half-state.
The habit that actually protects momentum
Write a one-line note before pausing a project — what you were about to do next — so resuming after exams takes minutes, not an hour of re-reading your own code to remember the plan.
See coding contests vs hackathons: the career trade-off for a related time-allocation decision.

posts.title: FAISS vs Qdrant vs pgvector: choosing a vector store for a student or startup RAG project
posts.description: Three vector stores I have actually used, compared on setup, filtering, persistence, hosting cost and when each one is the right call for a RAG project.
posts.text:
Students ask me which vector database to use far more often than they ask how to chunk, which is backwards — but the question deserves a straight answer. I have shipped with FAISS, Qdrant and pgvector. None is universally best; each is best at a stage.
FAISS: the fastest way to start
FAISS is a library, not a server. You build an index in memory, search it in microseconds, and save it to a file. It is perfect for prototypes, hackathons and offline evaluation. Its limits appear the moment you need metadata filtering ("only chunks from this document"), concurrent writes, or an index bigger than your RAM.
Qdrant: a real vector service
Qdrant runs as a service with a clean HTTP API, payload filtering, and persistence out of the box. For document-scoped RAG — a user asks questions about their own uploads only — its filtering is exactly what you need. It is one more container to run, which matters on small hosts; plan the memory budget.
pgvector: vectors next to your data
If your app already has PostgreSQL, pgvector adds a vector column and similarity operators to the database you are already backing up and querying. Joins between chunks and users, documents and permissions become ordinary SQL. It is the choice I reach for when the product has real users and real access control, because one database is easier to operate than two.
A decision table
Hackathon or notebook experiment → FAISS.
Multi-tenant RAG with per-document filtering and no existing database → Qdrant.
Product with users, permissions and PostgreSQL already in place → pgvector.
Corpus under 100k chunks and a single server → any of the three; optimise for operational simplicity.
The mistake to avoid
Choosing a vector store before you have an evaluation set. Retrieval quality is decided by chunking, embeddings and hybrid search — not by the database. Pick the store that fits your hosting and data model, then spend your effort on the pipeline in front of it.

posts.title: For placement cells: how industry GenAI sessions improve placements
posts.description: A guide for training and placement officers: which sessions change interview outcomes, how to schedule them across the year, what to ask speakers for, and how to turn one visit into internships.
posts.text:
Placement officers book AI sessions because companies are asking for AI skills, then watch students give the same interview answers as before. The sessions that change outcomes are specific, hands-on and timed to the placement calendar. Having spoken to students and reviewed hundreds of their projects, here is what I would schedule if I ran a placement cell.
Sessions that move interviews
Portfolio review clinics — a practitioner reviews ten student projects live and says what a recruiter would think. Students rewrite their READMEs that night. See portfolio over certificates.
Mock technical interviews for AI roles — the questions in GenAI engineer interview questions, with feedback on the answers.
A one-day build workshop — students leave with a deployed project to talk about; see a one-day GenAI workshop syllabus.
Honest career talks — what GenAI roles actually involve, from someone doing one, including the unglamorous parts.
Timing across the year
Start of the pre-final year: the build workshop, so projects exist by placement season.
Mid-year: portfolio clinics and mock interviews.
Two months before drives: a session on how to talk about projects — the story, the numbers, the trade-offs.
Final year, post-placement: sessions for the students still searching, focused on remote and startup roles (see getting a remote GenAI role from a tier-2 city).
What to ask speakers for
Specific feedback, not motivation. A rubric students can use on their own projects. A follow-up office hour. And an honest read on which students are ready — practitioners notice, and some of them hire or refer.
Turning a visit into internships
Ask the speaker whether their company or network takes interns, and have three students' portfolios ready to share the same day. SCULT INDIA has taken on students I met through sessions and communities; most practitioners have a similar story. The visit is the introduction; the placement cell's follow-up is what converts it.
Placement cells can arrange any of these formats through the invite page; sessions for student communities are free.

posts.title: Side project ideas that actually teach production skills, not just model-calling
posts.description: Calling an LLM API is the easy 10% of a real AI product. A list of side-project ideas chosen specifically to force the harder 90%.
posts.text:
Most student AI side projects stop at 'call the API, show the response' — which teaches almost nothing about the actual job of shipping a production AI system.
Project ideas chosen for what they force you to learn
A RAG app over your own college's documents — forces chunking, retrieval evaluation and a confidence gate, not just prompting.
A rate-limited public API wrapping a model — forces auth, rate limiting and cost control from day one.
A background-job pipeline processing uploaded documents — forces async architecture and error handling for slow tasks.
A small fine-tuned classifier deployed behind an API — forces the full train-evaluate-deploy loop, not just a notebook experiment.
The filter to apply to any project idea
Ask what it forces you to learn beyond calling an API. If the honest answer is 'nothing', pick a different project — the model call is rarely the part that teaches you anything a recruiter will ask about.
See shipping side projects that survive demo day.

posts.title: The hackathon demo that works live: a technical checklist
posts.description: How to make a demo survive the judging table: seeded data, a rehearsed path, offline fallbacks, no live deploys in the last hour, and what to say when something breaks anyway.
posts.text:
Demos fail at the worst moment because teams treat the demo as the last step instead of a feature. When I evaluate student projects, a live demo on real input is the single highest-weighted item on my rubric — so here is how to make sure yours runs.
Freeze early
Stop adding features two hours before judging. Use the time to run the demo path ten times, fix what breaks, and write down the exact sequence of clicks. The teams that lose points are usually the ones deploying a fix at minute fifty-nine.
The checklist
Seed the database with realistic data so the first screen is not empty.
Have one rehearsed path and one alternate path in case a judge asks for something different.
Run locally with a hotspot fallback; venue Wi-Fi is the most common single point of failure.
Cache or mock external APIs that are slow or rate-limited, and say so if asked.
Pre-load models and warm up any AI call before you are called; cold starts eat your three minutes.
Increase font size, zoom the browser, and close every other tab and notification.
Record a 60-second screen capture as a last-resort fallback — and label it as a recording if you use it.
Let the judge drive, briefly
Offer the judge one input of their choice. It costs thirty seconds and moves you from "demo on prepared input" to "live on judge input" on any serious rubric. Annapurna's demo at BYTEBATTLE let the panel post a real food listing; that moment did more than any slide.
When it breaks anyway
Say what broke, in one sentence, technically. "The geocoding API timed out; here is the cached response for the same address." Then continue. Judges score composure and understanding; a calm recovery often scores higher than a flawless demo from a team that cannot explain its own stack.
A demo is not the end of the build. It is the product you are shipping this weekend, and it deserves the same testing as anything else you would put in front of a user.

posts.title: TCS CodeVita 2025: complete preparation and registration guide
posts.description: How to register for TCS CodeVita, what the coding rounds actually test, and how to prepare no matter which degree you're in.
posts.text:
TCS CodeVita is one of the largest coding contests in the world and a direct gateway to TCS careers, placements and jobs. Every year I see the same three questions from students: how do I register, what's the syllabus, and how do I actually prepare.
Registration, in short
TCS opens registration on its official CodeVita portal ahead of the contest window. Register with a valid academic or personal email, complete your profile, and confirm your slot — the biggest mistake students make is registering the week of the deadline and missing the confirmation step.
What the rounds actually test
Data structures, algorithmic problem solving, and time-pressured debugging — less about knowing a niche technique, more about writing correct code fast under a countdown. Competitive programming fundamentals carry further here than clever tricks.
A preparation roadmap
Weeks 1-2: Refresh core data structures — arrays, strings, hashmaps, basic graphs.
Weeks 3-4: Timed practice sets, strictly under contest conditions, not open-book.
Week 5: Mock rounds mimicking the actual format, then a rest day before the real contest.
Why this matters beyond the contest
CodeVita is a direct opportunity for TCS internships and jobs, and it's a genuinely global competition — perfect for students from any degree who want a concrete data point for placement season beyond a GPA.
I made a full step-by-step video playlist covering registration, the preparation roadmap and practice strategy — linked below.

posts.title: How to read an AI research paper as a student without drowning in the math
posts.description: A practical reading order for a dense paper: abstract, figures, conclusion, then the method — and when it's fine to skip the proofs entirely.
posts.text:
Reading a paper front to back, in order, is the slowest and most discouraging way to extract what you actually need from it as a practitioner rather than a researcher.
A reading order that works
Abstract and conclusion first — what did they claim to show, and did it work.
Figures and tables next — most of a paper's real content lives in the results tables, not the prose around them.
The method section, skimmed for the core idea, not every equation.
Only then, if you need to reimplement something, the detailed math and proofs.
When it's fine to skip the proofs
If you're applying the idea, not proving a new theoretical result yourself, a solid intuitive understanding of why a method works is usually enough. Save full derivations for the rare paper whose core contribution you actually need to extend.
This reading habit pairs well with small language models: 1B-3B use cases as a paper-adjacent, practical starting point.

posts.title: How to evaluate a RAG system: recall, faithfulness and the questions that matter
posts.description: A practical evaluation setup for retrieval-augmented generation: build a question set, measure retrieval recall, grade faithfulness and refusal accuracy, and track it on every change.
posts.text:
You cannot improve a RAG system you are not measuring, and "I asked it five questions and it seemed fine" is not measuring. Every serious change I made to RAG.NextUpgrad — hybrid search, reranking, the confidence gate — was justified by a number moving on a fixed evaluation set. Here is the setup, sized for a student or a small team.
Build the question set first
Collect 50 to 100 real questions. For each, record the passage (and page) that answers it, and the expected answer in one sentence. Include 10 to 20 questions the documents cannot answer — those test whether the system refuses correctly. This set is your most valuable asset; version it alongside the code.
Four metrics, in order of importance
Retrieval recall@k — is the correct passage among the top k retrieved? If this is low, nothing downstream can save you. Fix chunking and retrieval before anything else.
Faithfulness — does every claim in the answer appear in the retrieved context? Grade it with a rubric, by hand for the first hundred answers and with an LLM judge afterwards, spot-checking the judge.
Refusal accuracy — on unanswerable questions, does the system say it does not know? On answerable ones, does it avoid refusing? A confidence gate is tuned entirely on this metric.
Answer correctness — does the answer match the expected one? Useful, but it hides whether a correct answer came from the documents or from the model's memory.
A minimal evaluation loop
Run the set on every change — a script that indexes, queries, and writes a CSV is enough. Track recall@5, faithfulness rate, false-refusal rate and false-answer rate over time. When a change improves one metric and hurts another, you have a real decision to make instead of an argument.
Traps I fell into
Writing questions by reading the documents, which produces questions phrased exactly like the text. Real users paraphrase; add paraphrased versions.
Grading with the same model that generated the answer, without checking the judge. Judges are lenient on fluent prose.
Evaluating only happy-path questions. The refusal set is where a production system earns trust.
A confidence gate without an evaluation set is a guess with a threshold. With one, it becomes the most defensible feature in the product — I explain the gate itself in why my RAG platform says "I don't know".

posts.title: Inviting a hackathon judge: what organisers should send in the first email
posts.description: How to invite a judge who will actually improve your hackathon: the brief, the rubric, the schedule, the number of teams, mentoring versus judging, and the small courtesies that make judges say yes again.
posts.text:
A judge who arrives knowing the theme, the rubric and the number of teams gives every team a fairer score and better feedback than one who is handed a clipboard at the door. Organisers control that entirely with the first email. Here is what mine should contain if you want the best session out of me — or any judge.
The brief
Event name, dates, venue or platform, and the organising body.
Theme and the actual problem statements.
Number of teams, team size, and how many the judge will see.
Pitch and Q&A timings.
Whether you want judging only, mentoring during the build, or both — and whether they are separated (see what a hackathon mentor actually does).
The rubric
Attach it, or ask the judge to help write one. A weighted rubric with descriptors, shared with teams in advance, is the single biggest improvement most college hackathons can make; there is one to copy in a hackathon judging rubric organisers can copy.
Logistics
A judges' briefing call or meeting before the first pitch — fifteen minutes to calibrate.
Submissions shared an hour before presentations.
A quiet space and a schedule that includes breaks; judging thirty teams is real work.
Travel and stay if on-site, or a stable video link and a co-host if remote.
What to ask the judge for
Written feedback for every team, two sentences each, tied to the rubric — the practice in how judges should give feedback. And five minutes after results for teams who want to ask questions. Judges who care will say yes; judges who will not are telling you something.
Courtesies that matter
The correct spelling of the judge's name on the certificate and the poster, a photograph with the winning teams, a public thank-you that names them, and the results announcement sent to them afterwards. These cost nothing and are why judges return.
I judge student hackathons on-site and remotely and bring the rubric above; the invitation details are on the campus invite page.

posts.title: Building a 'second brain' for learning AI: what to actually write down
posts.description: The GenAI field moves fast enough that notes decay within months. A practical note-taking system that stays useful instead of becoming a graveyard.
posts.text:
Most note-taking systems for a fast-moving field like GenAI turn into a graveyard of half-finished pages within a few months. The fix isn't a better app — it's a narrower, more deliberate scope.
What's worth writing down
A decision and its reasoning ('picked pgvector over a managed service because...') — these age well and are genuinely reusable.
A debugging story ('the model kept hallucinating dates until I added a confidence gate') — these teach more on reread than a summarised fact does.
A short, dated take on a fast-moving topic, explicitly flagged as likely to be outdated soon.
What to stop writing down
Copy-pasted documentation and tutorial summaries — these are one search away at any time and decay the moment the underlying tool updates. Your own reasoning and mistakes are the only notes that actually compound in value.
See writing your first technical blog post for turning these notes into something public.

posts.title: A hackathon judging rubric organisers can copy
posts.description: A complete, weighted rubric for student hackathons with scoring descriptors for each level, notes on calibrating judges, and how to publish criteria so teams build toward them.
posts.text:
Most college hackathons hand judges a sheet that says "Innovation (10), Technical (10), Presentation (10)" and hope for the best. The result is scores that depend on which judge a team drew. A usable rubric has weights, descriptors and a calibration step. Here is the one I offer organisers when I am invited to judge.
The criteria and weights
Problem and user (25%) — Is there a specific user with a specific pain? Did the team validate it, even by talking to five people?
Working solution (30%) — Does the demo run live on real input? How much of the claimed functionality is real versus mocked?
Engineering judgement (20%) — Were scope decisions deliberate? Are limitations stated honestly? Is the architecture appropriate rather than fashionable?
Communication (15%) — Can the team explain the problem, the solution and the trade-offs in three minutes, and answer questions directly?
Viability (10%) — Could this continue after the weekend? Is there a plausible next step?
Descriptors, so a 7 means the same thing to everyone
For each criterion write what a 2, a 5 and a 9 look like. For the demo: 2 is slides only; 5 is a demo on prepared input; 9 is a live demo on input the judge suggests. Descriptors turn opinions into observations and make feedback specific.
Calibrate the judges
Score the first two teams together and discuss differences before scoring the rest independently.
Agree what counts as "mocked" — a hard-coded response is a mock; a stubbed payment is fine.
Decide in advance how to treat teams that exceed time.
Publish it before the event
Teams build toward whatever they think is being scored. Publish the rubric with the problem statements and the quality of submissions rises across the board. It also removes the most common complaint after results — "we didn't know that mattered".
After the scores
Give every team two sentences of written feedback tied to a criterion. That is the part students keep. I wrote about doing it well in how judges should give feedback.
Organisers: take this rubric, adapt the weights to your theme, and if you want a judge who will use it and explain his scores to every team, write to pranjulrathour41@gmail.com.

posts.title: Reranking in RAG: why a cross-encoder second pass fixes most bad answers
posts.description: Bi-encoders retrieve fast but rank loosely. A cross-encoder reranker reads query and passage together and reorders the top candidates — here is how, what it costs, and when to skip it.
posts.text:
Vector search compares a query embedding to passage embeddings that were computed separately, so it never actually reads the query and the passage together. That is why it can rank a chunk about "refund policy for cancelled orders" above the one about "refund timelines" when a user asks how long refunds take. A reranker fixes exactly this gap.
What a cross-encoder does differently
A cross-encoder takes the query and one candidate passage as a single input and outputs a relevance score. Because it attends across both texts at once, it catches negations, specific entities and conditions that a bi-encoder blurs. The cost is that it must run once per candidate, so you never rerank the whole index — only the top 20 to 50 results from the first-stage retriever.
The two-stage pipeline
Retrieve broadly: hybrid dense + BM25 search returns the top 30 candidates (see hybrid retrieval explained).
Rerank precisely: score each candidate with the cross-encoder, keep the top 5.
Gate: if the best reranked score is below a threshold, refuse instead of answering (see what a confidence gate is).
Generate with citations from the surviving chunks only.
What it changed in RAG.NextUpgrad
Adding a reranker was the step that made the confidence gate trustworthy. Before it, first-stage scores were noisy enough that a threshold either blocked good answers or let weak ones through. Reranked scores separate relevant from irrelevant far more sharply, so the gate has something honest to measure. The platform still streams the answer token by token; the reranking pass adds a short pause before the first token, which users accept in exchange for fewer wrong answers.
Cost and latency, honestly
A small cross-encoder on CPU scores 30 passages in a few hundred milliseconds. On a free-tier server that is noticeable but fine; on GPU it is negligible. The memory footprint matters more than speed on small hosts — I covered that trade-off in the free-tier memory-budget playbook.
When to skip it
Your corpus is tiny and questions are simple — first-stage retrieval already puts the right chunk on top.
You have hard latency limits under 300 ms and no GPU.
Your evaluation set shows recall@5 above 95% without reranking. Measure before adding machinery.
If your RAG app gives confident wrong answers, add a reranker before you touch the prompt. In my experience it is the highest-leverage component after chunk

posts.title: Remote work etiquette for a student's first remote internship or job
posts.description: Remote work has unwritten rules nobody explains to a first-time remote employee. The habits that make a manager trust you were actually working.
posts.text:
A first remote internship comes with no orientation on the unwritten rules — habits that, done well, make a manager trust you're actually working without needing to check.
The habits that build trust remotely
Over-communicate status: a short daily update on what you did, even unprompted, replaces the visibility an office gives for free.
Respond within a reasonable window during agreed hours — silence for hours reads as absence, even if you're deep in focused work.
Ask questions in the team's shared channel, not only in DMs — it lets others learn from the answer too and shows you're engaged.
Turn your camera on for scheduled calls unless told otherwise; it's a small signal that reads as real presence.
The trap to avoid
Going quiet when stuck, hoping to solve it alone before anyone notices, is the single most common way trust erodes remotely. Ask for help sooner than feels comfortable — see how to ask a mentor for help for the exact phrasing that gets a fast, useful answer.

posts.title: A one-day GenAI workshop syllabus for colleges (hands-on, no fluff)
posts.description: A six-hour workshop plan that takes students from zero to a deployed retrieval-augmented app: prerequisites, four build blocks, the evaluation exercise, and what to send students afterwards.
posts.text:
Colleges ask for GenAI workshops and get slide decks about the history of neural networks. Students should leave a workshop with something running that they built, and a way to tell whether it works. This is the one-day plan I deliver, sized for 30 to 60 students with laptops.
Prerequisites, sent a week before
Python installed and a code editor working; a ten-minute check script provided.
A free account on an LLM provider, or keys supplied by the organisers for the day.
One PDF each student cares about — notes, a manual, a rulebook.
Block 1 (90 min): what a language model is, by using one
Live calls to a model from Python. Temperature, context, a prompt that fails and why. Students make three calls and break one on purpose. No slides for the first hour.
Block 2 (90 min): retrieval over your own document
Chunk the PDF, embed, search, answer with the retrieved text in the prompt. Each student runs it on their own document. The room sees hallucination disappear when context arrives — and reappear when retrieval misses, which sets up the afternoon.
Block 3 (60 min): making it honest
Add keyword search alongside vectors, add a threshold that refuses on weak matches, add a citation to the page. The ideas from what a confidence gate is in a form students can implement in an hour.
Block 4 (60 min): evaluate and deploy
Each student writes ten questions with known answers and scores their system. Then a minimal deploy so the demo has a URL. The workshop ends with everyone sharing a link and a score, not a certificate.
Afterwards
The complete code and a written version of every block.
One stretch task with a two-week deadline: add reranking, or swap the embedding model, and report what changed.
An office hour, remote, two weeks later for questions.
This syllabus is what I bring when a college books a full-day workshop; half-day and 90-minute versions exist. Details on the invite page.

posts.title: Building TechVerse Enclave: lessons from a 500-member developer community
posts.description: What actually works, and what flops, when you found and grow a student tech community while mentoring 200+ people through it.
posts.text:
I founded TechVerse Enclave in 2023 as a space for passionate minds across AI, web development, cybersecurity, data science and startups to learn, share and build together. It's since grown past 500 developers, and I've personally mentored 200+ students through it.
What the community actually offers
Knowledge sharing and resources.
Project collaboration and brainstorming.
Updates on events, hackathons and opportunities.
A network of like-minded tech professionals and learners, not just a chat group.
Formats that worked
Sessions with a live build on screen consistently outperformed slide-only talks — students showed up, stayed, and asked better questions when there was something concrete happening in front of them, whether that was a Changethon project showcase or a live AI mentorship demo.
Formats that flopped
Pure announcement posts with no substance behind them got engagement but no depth — people reacted, nobody built anything. The community grows on substance, not frequency.
If you want to start one on your campus
Start with five people who will actually show up, not fifty who might. TechVerse started as a small admin team — Raman Shukla, Saksham Gupta, Nikhil Tiwari, Bidhan Bhattacharya, Om Tripathi and me — before it was five hundred members.

posts.title: What hackathon judges actually look for: a rubric from both sides of the table
posts.description: The four things a judge is scoring in a three-minute pitch, why working demos beat ambitious slides, and the rubric Pranjul Rathour brings to a student hackathon panel.
posts.text:
I have pitched to judges at IIT Roorkee, CSJMU and a MeetKats hackathon and won; I have pitched STROT and lost. Now, when I sit on the other side of the table to evaluate student projects, I score what I wish I had understood as a participant. Judges are not looking for the most impressive stack. They are looking for four things, in roughly this order.
1. Did you solve a real problem for a real person?
The first thirty seconds decide whether the judge cares. Name the person, the situation and what goes wrong for them today. Krishi Gyan won Changethon 2025 because it started with a farmer who cannot read a dashboard, not with a diagram of a Gemini API call. If the judge cannot repeat your problem back in one sentence, the rest of the pitch is noise.
2. Does it work, live, right now?
A working demo of a narrow feature beats a slide deck about a broad platform every time. Judges have watched a hundred "imagine if" pitches. Show the thing doing the thing, with real input typed in front of them. If it breaks, say what broke and what you would fix — composure under a failed demo is itself a signal.
3. Did you make a deliberate trade-off?
Teams that cut scope on purpose and can explain why look like engineers. Teams that built everything half-way look like a to-do list. "We dropped the mobile app to get the matching logic right" is a sentence judges remember.
4. Can this team actually build it?
Who did what, and does the answer match the demo? A judge will ask one technical question to test whether the person answering understands the system. Let the person who built each part answer questions about it.
The rubric I bring to a panel
Problem clarity and user understanding — 25%
Working demo and technical execution — 30%
Scope judgement and honesty about limitations — 20%
Pitch clarity and answers under questioning — 15%
Feasibility beyond the weekend — 10%
Organisers are welcome to copy it; I share it in advance so no team is surprised. If your college is running a hackathon and wants a judge who will explain his scores, my invitation details are on the campus invite page.

posts.title: Negotiating your first tech offer as a student: what's actually negotiable
posts.description: Most first-time offers have more room than students assume, but not in the places students usually push on. A realistic guide to what to ask for.
posts.text:
Most students accept their first offer exactly as sent, assuming there's no room to negotiate. There usually is — just not always where you'd expect.
What's often negotiable
Joining date, if you have another commitment (exams, another interview) — companies flex on this more than on money.
Signing bonus or a one-time relocation allowance, even when base salary is fixed by a band.
Role or team placement, if the offer is generic and you have a specific interest area with relevant project work to show.
What's usually fixed
For entry-level roles, base salary bands are often genuinely fixed by policy — pushing hard here rarely moves the number and can read poorly for a first job. Ask, once, politely, and accept the answer.
The one rule that matters most: get everything agreed in writing before you resign from anything else or decline another offer.

posts.title: Chunking strategies for RAG: sizes, overlap and structure-aware splits
posts.description: How to split documents for retrieval-augmented generation: chunk sizes that retrieve precisely, overlap that preserves context, and structure-aware splitting for PDFs and code.
posts.text:
Most RAG quality problems I have debugged were chunking problems wearing a disguise. The model looked like it was hallucinating; the retriever was actually handing it half a table, or a paragraph whose subject lived in the previous chunk. Before you tune prompts or switch models, look at what your chunks actually contain.
Three rules that survive every project
Chunk for the question, not the document. A chunk should be able to answer a realistic user question on its own. For policy documents that is often 300–500 tokens; for API references it can be a single function signature plus its description.
Overlap is insurance, not a strategy. 10–15% overlap catches sentences that straddle a boundary. Larger overlaps mostly duplicate what the reranker sees and inflate your index.
Never split inside a structure. Tables, code blocks, numbered procedures and headings with their first paragraph belong together. Splitting them produces chunks that are individually meaningless.
Structure-aware splitting in practice
In RAG.NextUpgrad the ingest step first detects structure — headings, list runs, table rows — and only then applies a size budget. A heading is prepended to every chunk beneath it, so a chunk that says "the limit is 5 requests per second" also carries "Section 4.2: Rate limits". That single trick did more for answer accuracy than any embedding model change.
For scanned PDFs, run OCR page by page and keep page numbers as metadata. In the OCR & Speech Workspace every chunk records its page, which is what makes citations like "page 14" possible in the answer.
How to pick a size without guessing
Build a small evaluation set first: 30–50 real questions with the passage that answers each. Index the corpus at three chunk sizes (say 256, 512 and 1024 tokens), run the questions, and measure how often the correct passage appears in the top 5. The size that wins on recall is your starting point; then check answer quality, because a chunk that retrieves well can still be too fragmentary to answer from.
Signs your chunking is wrong
Answers that are correct but cite the wrong section — the heading context is missing.
Numbers quoted without their unit or condition — a table was split across chunks.
The model says "the document does not specify" for facts you know are there — the fact straddles a boundary and neither half ranks.
Retrieval scores are uniformly high — chunks are

posts.title: Answering 'tell me about a project' without rambling for five minutes
posts.description: The most common interview question also gets the worst answers — a chronological walkthrough with no point. A structure that fixes it in one pass.
posts.text:
'Tell me about a project' is the single most common interview question, and the single most commonly botched one — a chronological retelling of every step, with the interesting decision buried in minute four.
A structure that works
The problem, in one sentence: what wasn't working, for whom.
The interesting decision: the one trade-off or technical choice that actually mattered, and why you made it that way.
The result: what changed, ideally with a number.
One thing you'd do differently now — this signals growth, not weakness.
Practice the thirty-second version first
